title: Buffalo Bills WR Joshua Palmer could surprise in 2026
summary: Fans of the Buffalo Bills know that there will always be plenty of conversation around the wide receiver position. The team has one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL in Josh Allen, but there always seems to be room for conversation about whether the team has surrounded him with enough weapons. One of those […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 20: Joshua Palmer #5 of the Buffalo Bills runs during an NFL football game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on November 20, 2025 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Fans of the Buffalo Bills know that there will always be plenty of conversation around the wide receiver position. The team has one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL in Josh Allen, but there always seems to be room for conversation about whether the team has surrounded him with enough weapons. One of those weapons in 2025 was supposed to be wide receiver Joshua Palmer, who was the major investment made by president of football operations/general manager Brandon Beane. Things got off to a decent start in the Week 1 victory over the Baltimore Ravens, when Palmer had five receptions for 61 yards. Unfortunately, things seemed to sputter a bit after that — where injuries and some inconsistent play had Palmer finish the season with 22 receptions for 303 yards. The former third-round pick has been a bit of an afterthought this offseason, with most of the conversation focused on DJ Moore and Keon Coleman. Palmer was dealing with some nagging injuries during OTAs and mandatory minicamp, which didn’t help with the growing frustration from some fans (myself included). Conversations on social media questioned Palmer’s spot on the roster this season, with many speculating if a Brandin Cooks’ return was going to happen soon. While I feel that these questions were warranted and I could understand the frustration, Palmer reminded everyone on Saturday that he’s still one of the most-talented receivers on Buffalo’s roster. Anthony Prohaska from Cover 1 noted the following on Saturday: “ Josh Palmer is the best route runner amongst the Bills WRs. If he stays healthy, he’ll be a useful part of the rotation. And addling DJ Moore allows Palmer to operate in roles and spaces that are better for his skillset.“ Similar sentiments were shared by those in attendance, with the official Bills social media accounts sharing video footage of a highlight play from Allen to Palmer. While one practice doesn’t mean that everything will work out for Palmer this season, it does serve as a reminder that Palmer could be a valuable member of Buffalo’s offense.
author: Anthony Marino

title: Buffalo Bills rookie LB Kaleb Elarms-Orr turning heads at training camp
summary: Have the Buffalo Bills found another Day 3 gem via the NFL Draft? It sure feels like that’s the case with rookie linebacker Kaleb Elarms-Orr, even if it’s wise to pump the brakes as players have yet to put on pads at training camp. Still, when speaking of Elarms-Orr, it’s difficult not to get excited […]
full_text: Jun 9, 2026; Orchard Park, NY, USA; Buffalo Bills linebacker Kaleb Elarms-Orr (52) trains during Buffalo Bills Minicamp. Mandatory Credit: Gregory Fisher-Imagn Images | Gregory Fisher-Imagn Images Have the Buffalo Bills found another Day 3 gem via the NFL Draft? It sure feels like that’s the case with rookie linebacker Kaleb Elarms-Orr, even if it’s wise to pump the brakes as players have yet to put on pads at training camp. Still, when speaking of Elarms-Orr, it’s difficult not to get excited about his talent and potential, and the opportunity continuously staring him in the face. The Bills are implementing a new 3-4 base defense favored by first-time NFL defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard. A former Bills safety in his playing days, Leonhard comes in seeking to attack opponents. It’s a sizeable paradigm shift to many players who, for many years, operated out of former head coach Sean McDermott’s discipline-based, zone-heavy “Buffalo Nickel” system. Among those carryovers from McDermott’s tenure are presumptive starting inside linebackers Terrel Bernard and Dorian Williams. When healthy, both players have given the Bills plenty of production on defense. The caveat is of course the matter of health, where both have seen more than their fair share of injuries. In fact, Bernard and Williams are currently under a workload management plan because of injuries. For Bernard, he’s coming off surgery earlier this offseason to repair a serious ankle injury sustained during the 2025 NFL season — something that slowed down last season’s lone defensive captain, limiting his previously explosive nature all season. As for Williams, he sustained an injury during Organized Team Activities (OTAs), and was seen using crutches. Williams revealed at the start of this season’s training camp that he suffered a bilateral knee fracture , which implies that both knees were affected. Add it all up, and the grass sure does seem pretty green right now for a savvy first-year linebacker looking to leave a good impression on his coaches. That’s precisely what Elarms-Orr has done since being drafted by One Bills Drive 126th overall in Round 4. It was a bit of a surprise that Elarms-Orr dropped so far this past April given the pre-draft buzz he generated. It probably surprised Buffalo’s key decision makers too, who played their hand well in landing him fairly late in the process. In fact, Elarms-Orr was the only linebacker Buffalo selected in the draft. A heady, instinctual, bona fide sideline-to-sideline linebacker, the 2025 First Team All-Big 12 honors TCU linebacker clearly piqued the Bills’ interest, hosting him on a Top-30 pre-draft visit. In the draft’s lead-up, many wondered if Elarms-Orr would be selected with Buffalo’s top pick this past April. To this point, it’s a move that’s paid off well for the team. Whether during minicamps or OTAs, Elarms-Orr has turned heads with his depth of knowledge, especially so in terms of Leonhard who’s praised his on-field efficiency and the ability to almost always be in the right spot for the defense. Earlier this spring Leonhard pointed out to reporters that Elarms-Orr picked up the defense well off the bat, even showing well in a communication role while controlling the huddle. No one can deny that Elarms-Orr has taken advantage of the massive opportunity presented to him during the spring and early summer, which Leonhard pointed out in an early press conference. "He's taken advantage of a huge opportunity." #Bills 4th round pick Kaleb Elarms-Orr has been running with the 1st team with Terrel Bernard and Dorian Williams working back from injury. DC Jim Leonhard with high praise early for the rookie. "He doesn't blink." pic.twitter.com/tilFfDlLJo — Jon Scott (@JonScottTV) July 30, 2026 He’ll have to earn every snap but Elarms-Orr hasn’t looked back since picking up the ball, having seen run with the defensive ones beginning with those early sessions and now continuing to do so with the first week of training camp now in the books. He’s been observed working long after practice ends to refine his technique and claim as many reps as possible toward making an immediate impact in his first season. Dating back to those OTA sessions, Elarms-Orr told Ian Mills of News10NBC that he “want(s) to be the starter Week 1. ” "I wanna be the starter week one." #Bills rookie LB Kaleb Elarms-Orr is positioned to, at the very least, play a lotta snaps this year. The fourth-rounder says he wants to be on first team for week one. Jim Leonhard had some praise for the TCU product last week. #BillsMafia pic.twitter.com/DXjbFxV5Bu — Ian Mills (@IanMillsTV) June 2, 2026 Like any rookie, every day provides a new chance for Elarms-Orr to learn and develop. On Day 3 of training camp this past Saturday, Elarms-Orr was lined up at starting MIKE with Bernard at starting WILL for team drills. Then later, it was Dorian Williams in at starting MIKE alongside Bernard at WILL for 7-on-7 work. Though Williams is now healthy, it’s reasonable to expect that Buffalo’s new defensive coaching staff isn’t resting on its laurels while trying to find the best players to fit their intended scheme. There’s still much left for Elarms-Orr to learn, which is of course true for any Bills defender making the transition to play in Leonhard’s system. That Elarms-Orr has come in with such drive, determination, and on-field physicality speaks to his innate abilities. The valuable experience Elarms-Orr’s gained early in the process should only pay dividends — if not now, then perhaps down the road but sooner than many could have predicted. Beyond Bernard, Williams, and Elarms-Orr, the Bills are relatively thin at linebacker. The room is rounded out by Joe Andreessen, Jimmy Ciarlo, Theron Gaines, Demetrius Flannigan-Fowles, and Keonta Jenkins. Neither among veteran linebackers Matt Milano or Shaq Thompson have been re-signed despite both playing significant roles in 2025. In a vacuum, the current linebacker room seems to paint a fairly clear path to potentially substantial playing time for Elarms-Orr. The football world knows that one play can change everything, which means health and availability is likely to be among the main factors in picking a starting pair among Bernard, Williams, and Elarms-Orr. There are three preseason exhibitions to get through, and it’s likely that trio sees extended run with the ones to properly diagnose the team’s starting linebacker prospects. When the dust settles, could Elarm-Orr be in line to wear a green dot as a rookie? If so, it’s something that hasn’t happened since 2018, when the Bills drafted linebacker Tremaine Edmunds.
author: Matt Byham

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: S Jalon Kilgore
summary: The Buffalo Bills have needed to add dynamic athletes to their defense for some time. Especially in the defensive secondary, a reliance on drafting corners whose best fit was to play zone coverage led to repeated issues against elite teams, and those issues often cropped up at the most inopportune times — like during the […]
full_text: COLUMBIA, SC - NOVEMBER 29: Jalon Kilgore #24 of the South Carolina Gamecocks intercepts a pass in the end zone in front of Adam Randall #8 of the Clemson Tigers during a college football game on November 29, 2025 at Williams-Brice Stadium in Columbia, South Carolina. (Photo by Joe Robbins/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Buffalo Bills have needed to add dynamic athletes to their defense for some time. Especially in the defensive secondary, a reliance on drafting corners whose best fit was to play zone coverage led to repeated issues against elite teams, and those issues often cropped up at the most inopportune times — like during the playoffs. While the team began to add different types of athletes over the final two years of former head coach Sean McDermott’s tenure, those players were still playing in his zone-heavy system. Now, a new defensive coordinator in Jim Leonhard has the reins. Will his defense be an attacking, aggressive scheme as advertised? Does that mean more man coverage, more blitzing, or more of the same with a few tweaks here and there? In today’s installment of our “91 players in 91 days” series, we discuss a rookie who has a chance to become a key piece in Leonhard’s new-look Buffalo defense. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Jalon Kilgore Number: 29 Position: S Height/Weight: 6’1”, 210 pounds Age: 21 (22 on 1/27/2027) Experience/Draft: R; selected by Buffalo in the fifth round (No. 167 overall) of the 2026 NFL Draft College: South Carolina Acquired: Fifth-round draft choice Financial situation (per Spotrac): Kilgore enters the first year of his four-year rookie contract, which is worth $4,843,324 overall. For the 2026 season, his cap hit is $1,000,831 if he makes the 53-man roster; Buffalo will carry a dead-cap charge of $463,324 if he’s released. 2025 Recap: Kilgore followed up his phenomenal sophomore campaign with yet another strong season as a junior. Playing in 11 games, he totaled 54 tackles, which was good for fourth on the team. Kilgore missed one game due to a hamstring injury. He tied for the team lead in interceptions with two, and he led the team in pass breakups with 10. Before the season began, he was one of five players voted a permanent team captain by his teammates, and after the season, he earned plenty of accolades as a result of his stellar play. He was named to multiple All-SEC teams, including Phil Steele (Third Team), the SEC Coaches (Second Team), and PFSN (First Team). He was also voted co-Defensive MVP. He was invited to the 2026 NFL Scouting Combine, and he put on a show. Kilgore is an elite athlete, and he didn’t disappoint at the combine. He ran the 40-yard dash in 4.4 seconds and the 20-yard shuttle in 4.32 seconds, bench pressed 225 pounds a total of 16 times, and leapt 37” in the vertical jump, and 10’10” in the broad jump. According the the Relative Athletic Score (RAS) metric, Kilgore is the fifth-highest scorer at strong safety since 1987, scoring a 9.97 RAS out of 10. Positional outlook: Kilgore is one of six players listed at safety on the current roster. C.J. Gardner-Johnson, Cole Bishop, Damar Hamlin, Geno Stone, and Wande Owens are the others. Sam Franklin is listed as a defensive back, and while he is technically a safety, his real position is on special teams. Jordan Hancock is also listed at defensive back, and he might play slot corner or safety. 2026 Offseason: Kilgore is healthy and he participated in offseason workouts. 2026 Season outlook: Of all the selections Buffalo made on defense in April’s draft, it’s Kilgore that excites me the most. He is exactly what the Bills need in the back third of the defense, as they’ve needed to infuse the defensive secondary with more athletic players for quite some time. It’s something that the team recognized and began doing last offseason, but they’ve moved towards faster players in general on defense over the last 12 months. Part of me doesn’t understand why Kilgore fell all the way to the fifth round of the NFL Draft. He’s a three-year starter in the SEC who has performed quite well, starting 33 games in his NCAA career. There are some questions about his positional fit in the NFL, as he played more of a big nickel or “Star” defender for the Gamecocks, and that role could limit him as a pro. Does he have the agility and the fluidity to stay with receivers over the middle? Does the have the ability to backpedal and react to deep threats as a deep-third safety? Those are certainly questions to be answered; however, based on his overall athletic profile and his success in college, my thought is that he’ll be able to perform at various levels of the defense. Todd McShay at The Ringer compared him to Derwin James , with the caveat that Kilgore doesn’t have the same high-end game tape that made James a first-round pick. They note him as a low-floor, high-ceiling pick, writing that he’ll likely begin his career as a rotational defensive back and special teams contributor before eventually developing into a starter. That’s probably the ideal pathway here in Buffalo, as Gardner-Johnson and Bishop will start at safety for the Bills when they’re healthy. Will Kilgore do enough to push for time as the third safety? Is he competing with someone like Hancock for snaps on defense as a big nickel/dime back hybrid? Time will tell, but Leonhard should have fun using a big chess piece like Kilgore on defense this season. Not only do I think he makes the roster, but I think that, by the end of the year, he’s making a case for being the best rookie defender on the club.

title: Plays That Defined 2025: Philadelphia Eagles, Week 17
summary: The 2025 Buffalo Bills’ season has been written, but the book is incomplete. Before we cast our full attention toward the 2026 season, let’s take one last glance back over our shoulder for our annual look at the Plays That Defined the prior campaign. For any newcomers, first and foremost; Welcome! When it comes to […]
full_text: The 2025 Buffalo Bills’ season has been written, but the book is incomplete. Before we cast our full attention toward the 2026 season, let’s take one last glance back over our shoulder for our annual look at the Plays That Defined the prior campaign. For any newcomers, first and foremost; Welcome! When it comes to the “rules” of this exercise, we’re not voting for our favorite highlight necessarily, but the one that best captures the essence of the game. Put differently, if you had to choose just one play to show someone to explain as much of the contest as possible, which would you choose? Week 17; Philadelphia Eagles at Buffalo Bills Sometimes it’s just not your day. On a rainy winter day (the literal worst weather for being in the stands), the Bills had the stats for a victory. They had nearly twice as many first downs as the Eagles (20 to 11), half a yard per rush better on the ground, and nearly two-and-a-half times the passing yardage. Buffalo held the ball for over 10 minutes more than Philadelphia. The Bills had only one turnover. So what happened? The bad plays were all just at the worst time. Well, on offense that is. The defense held pretty strong all game. Josh Allen and company looked like self-defeating gremlins and still almost pulled out a win. Very depressing. It’s a good thing nothing lasts forever, even cold December rain. Sack and fumble (Q1; 4:10) Plays That Defined 2025 – Week 17 – Sack and Fumble pic.twitter.com/Tbqn251JDi — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) July 8, 2026 If there was one common thread in Philadelphia stopping Buffalo, it might be sacks. Of the five, this is for sure the worst. What with the fumble and the next drive resulting in the Eagles’ one touchdown and all. Blocked extra point (Q4; 5:11) Plays That Defined 2025 – Week 17 – Blocked extra point pic.twitter.com/HO87jGwxBJ — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) July 8, 2026 When you lose by one point they’re all pretty important. Not only did this blocked extra point directly remove one off the scoreboard, but it was probably also a factor into another play lower down the list. This was Michael Badgley’s second and last game with Buffalo and while this wasn’t entirely his fault, Bills fans were glad to see 67-year old Matt Prater back the next week. Last stop (Q4; 3:36) Plays That Defined 2025 – Week 17 – Last stop pic.twitter.com/ND1LnE9av9 — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) July 8, 2026 As noted, the Bills’ defense held up quite well in this game. I had several stops to choose from, but elected to go with their final stop. This allowed the offense to take the field again to drive for the tie or win. Trick play (Q4; 1:51) Plays That Defined 2025 – Week 17 – A fun play pic.twitter.com/WpnoHvKPtJ — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) July 8, 2026 Will this actually be a play I put in the poll to vote on, or is it here just because it’s fun and we could use a bit of fun in these things? Stay tuned! Failed two-point try (Q4; 0:05) Plays That Defined 2025 – Week 17 – Failed two point try pic.twitter.com/xIbCP9AZ4r — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) July 8, 2026 Ahem. Deep inhale… AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHH! Which play best defines the Bills’ loss?

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 41 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change […]
full_text: Carolina Panthers center Jeff Mitchell sets to block against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers November 6, 2005 in Tampa. The Panthers defeated the Bucs 34 - 14. (Photo by Al Messerschmidt/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #41. Jeff Mitchell Panthers stats: 78 games, 78 starts Career stats: 119 games, 118 starts After a stellar college career at Florida, center Jeff Mitchell was a fifth-round pick by the Baltimore Ravens in 1997. His career got off to a slow start as he didn’t see the field in his rookie season, but that quickly changed. Over the next three seasons he started 40 games for the Ravens. In his final season with the Ravens in 2000, Baltimore won the Super Bowl with Mitchell starting throughout the regular season and playoffs. After winning the Super Bowl, Jeff Mitchell signed with the Carolina Panthers in 2001. And if you’re a Panthers historian, you’ll ruefully recall the Panthers went 1-15 that year. Immediately after hoisting the Lombardi Trophy, Mitchell was snapping the ball to Chris Weinke for the league’s worst team while trying to open holes for running backs Richard Huntley (165 carries), Nick Goings (66), and the immortal Tim Biakabutuka (53). Talk about the best of times and the worst of times. But things would get much better for Jeff Mitchell from there. Over the next four seasons from 2002-2005 Carolina went 36-28, including two 11-win seasons and a Super Bowl appearance in 2003. Stalwart players from the 2003 Super Bowl squad like Mitchell deserve a place of respect in the minds of Panthers fans, and that’s exactly what he’s getting today. Over five seasons with the Panthers he started all 78 regular season games in which he played, missing just two games over that stretch. While he never made the Pro Bowl in his career, he was a capable, steady, and solid at center. Good centers make the entire offensive line better and make life easier for their quarterbacks, and Mitchell was very good at that for half a decade in Carolina.

title: Will Patrick Jones II be the next man up?
summary: The Carolina Panthers signed Patrick Jones II during the 2025 free agency period to bolster a pass rushing unit that had been struggling for years. The plan was for him to have the opportunity to take the next step forward as a starter in the NFL while providing a strong veteran presence for the rookies […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 5: Patrick Jones II #91 of the Carolina Panthers runs onto the field during player introductions prior to the game against the Miami Dolphins at Bank of America Stadium on October 5, 2025 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Carolina Panthers signed Patrick Jones II during the 2025 free agency period to bolster a pass rushing unit that had been struggling for years. The plan was for him to have the opportunity to take the next step forward as a starter in the NFL while providing a strong veteran presence for the rookies that the Panthers would ultimately select in the next month’s NFL Draft. Part of that plan held up to contact with the rest of the season. The Panthers drafted Nic Scourton and Princely Umanmielen with the 51st and 77th overall picks. Jones started four games for the Panthers before requiring a season ending back surgery. His absence allowed Scourton to flourish with an expanded role and develop into a fan favorite and potential star of the 2026 season. Scourton didn’t even make it out of training camp before suffering his own season ending injury this season. Panthers fans are now largely expecting Jones to step back into his starting role from last season and fill the gap until Scourton’s ultimate return. This is the obvious answer to the Reacts question we posed last week, but it is not an answer that is guaranteed to satisfy Panthers fans once the season actually starts. Jones only has nine starts and 13 sacks in his five years in the league, including his injury-shortened year with the Panthers. He had seven sacks in his contract year with the Minnesota Vikings, showing the potential that earned him his free agency contract with Carolina. But that potential is really all we have to work with right now when projecting Jones’ 2026 season. Until he or Umanmielen can capitalize on their potentials, it may well be that signing Jaelen Phillips and losing Scourton to injury may be another case of one step forward, one step back for defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero’s perennially hamstrung defense. title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 42 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #42: S Colin Jones Well this one just so happens to coincide with the jersey number, as we celebrate former safety/cornerback and special teams player, The Ace That Runs The Place COLIN JONES! Jones was drafted in the 6th round of the 2011 NFL Draft by the San Francisco 49ers, and spent one season there before the Panthers acquired him in August of 2012, shipping off a 2014 7th round pick for his services. This transaction turned out to be a bargain, as Colin Jones played in 124 games as a Panther from 2012 to 2019 in various capacities, mostly as a special teams ace, but he did start 14 games as either a spot starter at safety, and even as a nickel cornerback at times in a pinch. Jones logged 3 interceptions and 7 pass deflections when called upon in these duties, but he will always be remembered as a special teams player, and a stalwart one for this team. I know, I know, there’s likely going to be booing in the comment section. But, I have prepared my arguments for why Colin Jones belongs on this list. First of all, in the two seasons Colin Jones started 3 or more games (2015-3 starts, 2017-7 starts), the Panthers made the playoffs! Secondly, Colin Jones is the second most veteran DEFENSIVE BACK in Carolina Panthers history with 124 games played for the franchise, trailing only Mike Minter with 148 games played. He is the 7th most veteran defender in general for the Panthers, trailing only Thomas Davis, Julius Peppers, Mike Minter, Charles Johnson, Mike Rucker, and Jason Kyle in games played for the franchise. The Ace That Runs The Place is low-key one of the better trades the Panthers have ever made, trading away a 7th round pick two years out from the transaction. What they got was a special teams ace who stepped in to whatever role was needed when called upon, and spent 7 seasons in Carolina doing so. While fans often wanted to see him released during that time for the shiny, new undrafted free agents to serve as safety 4/5 on the depth chart, I truly hope the heart has grown fonder now that we can look back half a decade later at his services. And we’ll always have this crazy interception , and his run on a fake punt . When all was said and done, Jones very much embodied the Keep Pounding philosophy in the sense of simply doing the job he was asked of, even if it was doing something like playing nickel corner since the Panthers didn’t value depth corners during the large portion of his career. Maybe that’s on the coaches, or maybe they had the knowledge that the answer was on the roster already. Either way, celebrate the Ace down below!

title: Cash, Stash, or Slash: Tyrique Stevenson
summary: As we continue to look at potential candidates for extensions or roster turnover, we switch back to the defense, and we look at Tyrique Stevenson. Stevenson quickly became a fan favorite throughout his rookie season and kicked off year number two with a Pick Six against the Tennessee Titans. The sky was the limit for […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 18: Tyrique Stevenson #29 of the Chicago Bears holds the football after a play during an NFL divisional playoff football game against the Los Angeles Rams at Soldier Field on January 18, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images As we continue to look at potential candidates for extensions or roster turnover, we switch back to the defense, and we look at Tyrique Stevenson. Stevenson quickly became a fan favorite throughout his rookie season and kicked off year number two with a Pick Six against the Tennessee Titans. The sky was the limit for Stevenson, but since that Pick Six, he’s spent far too much time at his floor than his ceiling. Stevenson has been wildly inconsistent with serious lapses in concentration during games. He’s had coaches call out his lack of consistency (with both coaching staffs), and despite being what should be a great fit, he hasn’t shined like many thought he would in Dennis Allen’s defense. Tyrique Stevenson: Slash With the three years he’s put in so far, there’s absolutely zero chance the Bears will give Stevenson an extension heading into the 2026 season. Stevenson will be an unrestricted free agent in March of 2027, but the question is, is there any way the Bears do something with Stevenson before he reaches free agency? Some of you might want to put Stevenson in the “Stash” category. What if Stevenson has a big year? What if Stevenson finally breaks out and becomes “the man?” I say, even if he does, I think there’s too much baggage to give out significant cash to Stevenson no matter how well he plays. If Stevenson is a borderline Pro Bowl candidate and looks like he finally put it together, is it worth the Bears ponying up some sort of contract that would probably be in the ballpark of a 3-year deal worth around $15 or $16 million per season, maybe more? The Bears would probably have to guarantee Stevenson about 2 years of that contract as well. Should they be willing to do that? Can you be confident that after you pay Stevenson, he will continue to be focused and play consistently? After three of the four years he was with Chicago, that was not the case. I think Stevenson goes a similar path to Brisker. Last year we talked about Brisker and if he played well, would he be worth bringing back, despite the concussion issues in the past. Brisker didn’t get paid much at all by the Pittsburgh Steelers, which means the Bears easily could have brought him back, but they moved on. Now Stevenson is a better fit for this defense than Brisker is, but regardless, it was pretty obvious before last season that Brisker was going to be gone after 2025 no matter how he played. Stevenson has those vibes right now. He is most likely going to start this year despite losing his job last year simply because there isn’t a lot behind him that can push for a starting job this season. Stevenson showed plenty of promise, but the lows are what are going to push him off the roster. Even if he rebounds and has a great season, it’s not worth throwing a contract his way; there’s just too high a chance that it’ll bite you in the butt. If Stevenson leaves and gets a decent contract and goes on to great things, great for Tyrique, but it’s simply too high a risk to see if that can happen in Chicago.

title: Ja’Marr Chase knows what he and the Bengals need to do to recapture 2021 magic
summary: Every Cincinnati Bengals fan has heard or thought about how this offseason feels very similar to 2021. This offseason, the Bengals were heavily active in free agency after a disastrous season the year before, much like how active they were in free agency in 2021 after Joe Burrow got his knee shredded 10 games into […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - DECEMBER 26: Cincinnati Bengals wide receiver Ja'Marr Chase (1) runs with the football during a game between the Cincinnati Bengals and the Baltimore Ravens on December 26, 2021, at Paul Brown Stadium in Cincinnati, OH. (Photo by Robin Alam/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Every Cincinnati Bengals fan has heard or thought about how this offseason feels very similar to 2021. This offseason, the Bengals were heavily active in free agency after a disastrous season the year before, much like how active they were in free agency in 2021 after Joe Burrow got his knee shredded 10 games into his rookie season in 2020. In addition, the schedule this season has many parallels to the 2021 schedule: Week 1 at home against an NFC opponent, Week 3 at Pittsburgh at 1:00, Week 4 at home against Jacksonville. Sound familiar? It should. But the biggest thing about the 2021 Bengals was how explosive they were offensively, how easy they made it look to air the ball out and take the top off the defense. Even with the success of the last four seasons on offense, they haven’t been as explosive on that side of the ball. Ja’Marr Chase knows this, and he made it clear to start training camp that the Bengals need to recapture their explosive nature offensively, the same explosive offense that got former Baltimore Ravens defensive coordinator Don Martindale fired after the 2021 season. “Defenses are adjusting to us,” Chase stated. “That’s what they’re supposed to do. It’s our job for us to get better, be better than last year, and make those adjustments to be more explosive. “We’ve just got to see it, recognize it and be able to adjust for the next play.” In that 2021 season, the Bengals put up 41 points on the Ravens in both games. Joe Burrow threw for 941 combined yards and seven touchdowns. Ja’Marr Chase had 15 receptions for 326 yards and a touchdown. “Me and Joe are already talking about how we can make explosives,” Chase said. “And when I finally get it in camp, it’s just, how can I react to it when I see it in the game? So, we’re practicing now, and when the game comes, we see it and attack it. And it’s explosive.” If the Bengals can take the top off defenses this season, good luck trying to stop them on offense. With all five starters returning on the offensive line, that could lead to more plays that take time to unfold down the field. If Burrow can sit in the pocket and let Chase fly down the field, good luck trying to keep the top on your defense.

title: Bengals training camp Day 5 News and discussion
summary: We have seen a bit of fight from the defense early in training camp from the Cincinnati Bengals defense. The team certainly did quite a bit to improve that side of the ball in the offseason, and we have seen that show up in Boye Mafe making some early pressures. However, we have also seen […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 12: Defensive coordinator Al Golden of the Cincinnati Bengals looks on during the first quarter in the game against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field on October 12, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images We have seen a bit of fight from the defense early in training camp from the Cincinnati Bengals defense. The team certainly did quite a bit to improve that side of the ball in the offseason, and we have seen that show up in Boye Mafe making some early pressures. However, we have also seen players like Demetrius Knight Jr. and Barrett Carter make plays at linebacker. Is it time to panic about the offense? Definitely not. Quarterback Joe Burrow has still had moments of absolute brilliant ball placement, and there were days like this even last offseason when the defense got the better of them. This is the time to experiment with some things, and Burrow and company are doing plenty of that. Let us know in the comments your feeling on this year’s squad after a few days of training camp to digest. Bengals News Training Camp Report | Boye Mafe Finds A Home; Erick All Jr.’s Wait Ends Monday “One thing about me, I’m out there working trying to crack my craft,” Mafe said. “Camp is where you fine-tune your craft. You work all summer on different moves, different ways to elevate your game. See what works, see what doesn’t work, see what you can take into the season.” Mafe is carrying plenty of expectations to see his production expand with a bigger role. His current approach suggests it is a good bet for the team to make. The entire defense improving obviously involves more than him stepping up, but him becoming an EDGE who can consistently pressure the quarterback is a fairly large piece of that. Quick Hits | Jalen Davis Strikes Again; Connor Lew Debut; 2 Cincy Kids At Camp “You get the happy nerves. I haven’t had contact since the end of October,” said Lew, alluding to the torn ACL he suffered against Missouri. “We’re at the stage where we’re not ahead of schedule or behind schedule. It’s just day-to-day, and they told me I could go out there and get full-speed contact. It felt really good.” Davis certainly keeps having his name pop up. The first was the scuffle he and wide receiver Ja’Marr Chase had on Day 1 of training camp. This time he made an opportune turnover. He has never made it easy on this coaching staff to cut him, but now he is making it hard for them to keep him off the field. Why Bengals keep dropping Boye Mafe, Cashius Howell in pass coverage “That’s something I am trying to work on to get more comfortable with,” Howell told Geoff Hobson of Bengals.com. “My primary thing is rushing the passer and playing on the line of scrimmage, but that is something I am trying to actively work on and actively make sure I’m getting better at day by day.” It does make sense that Mafe and Howell are not as prolific in coverage as they are rushing the passer. It also feels like offenses have caught up to this tactic. Namely players like Burrow, Patrick Mahomes, Josh Allen… ect., all have seen this for years now. It is nice to sprinkle in, but the key is you need to be able to rush the passer into making a mistake when you drop a defensive lineman into coverage. If you can’t then the quarterback just has to wait for a receiver to find the hole in whatever zone that lineman is covering. Mafe and Howell are never going to be good enough in coverage to make a play defensively if the quarterback has all day to throw. To try and make the point a bit clearer. If Mafe and Howell are considered to have a D in coverage, they are good enough as a surprise defensive lineman if the quarterback has to act quickly because of pass rush. Them becoming a D+ or even C graded in coverage is not enough of an increase for them to be good enough if the quarterback has even a decent amount of time in the pocket. Bengals’ Early-Season Test Just Got Tougher After Texans’ Latest Move Clowney gives Houston another proven weapon to unleash against Joe Burrow and Cincinnati’s offensive line. Danielle Hunter and Will Anderson Jr. combined for 27 sacks last season, leaving Houston with two defenders capable of taking over a game from opposite sides of the defensive front. While it is unfortunate an already good defense gets better in the AFC. There were reports that Clowney was also talking with the Cleveland Browns about a return. Even without Myles Garrett, that defensive line is still fairly scary with Jared Verse taking his spot. So they will only have to see him once on a loaded defensive line instead of twice.
author: Patrick Judis

title: Ted Karras’ latest comments show just how quickly Dexter Lawrence is changing the Bengals
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals made one of the biggest splashes of the 2026 offseason when they acquired All-Pro defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence II. Through just a handful of training camp practices, it’s already becoming apparent that the veteran’s impact extends well beyond what he’ll do on Sundays. No one knows that better than veteran center Ted […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - OCTOBER 13: Dexter Lawrence II #97 of the New York Giants and the defensive line lines up against Ted Karras #64 of the Cincinnati Bengals and the offensive line during an NFL game at MetLife Stadium on October 13, 2024 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals made one of the biggest splashes of the 2026 offseason when they acquired All-Pro defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence II. Through just a handful of training camp practices, it’s already becoming apparent that the veteran’s impact extends well beyond what he’ll do on Sundays. No one knows that better than veteran center Ted Karras. Speaking with reporters following Saturday’s practice, Karras offered glowing praise for Lawrence after spending the first week of camp battling him in the trenches. “Better bring your f-ing shit when you’re going against Dexter Lawrence.” Ted Karras being texted daily against the stud DT. Karras compared it to going up against the 2016 Patriots in practice. pic.twitter.com/fPSXYFBe9y — Mike Petraglia (@Trags) August 1, 2026 “Better bring your f-ing stuff when you’re going against Dexter Lawrence.” That’s about as strong of an endorsement as an offensive lineman can give. Karras went on to compare the challenge of practicing against Lawrence to facing the loaded defensive fronts he experienced during his time with the New England Patriots, emphasizing just how much the four-time Pro Bowler is elevating the level of competition every single day. Iron sharpens iron Training camp often revolves around one simple football cliché: Iron sharpens iron. In Cincinnati, that saying appears to be coming to life. Lawrence has consistently disrupted plays throughout the opening practices, forcing the Bengals’ offensive line to match his intensity. Rather than viewing it as a nuisance, Karras sees it as exactly what this team needs. Earlier this offseason, Karras called Lawrence “probably the best nose tackle in the last 30 years,” praising his rare combination of size, power and athleticism. After finally sharing the practice field with him every day, it doesn’t sound like he’s changed his opinion one bit. Karras also believes the daily battles are helping mold what could become the best run-blocking offensive line he’s been a part of in Cincinnati. If the Bengals’ offense can consistently move one of the NFL’s premier defensive tackles in practice, Sundays against opposing defenses should feel a bit easier. Setting a new tone on defense Lawrence’s influence has been noticeable almost immediately. Whether it’s stuffing runs, celebrating with emphatic energy after a stop, or pushing teammates to compete harder, the 350-pound defensive tackle has brought an edge that has been evident throughout camp. That competitive fire has even spilled over into some spirited exchanges with Karras, though both veterans have made it clear it’s all rooted in making each other better. It’s exactly the type of leadership Cincinnati hoped it was acquiring. A promising early sign Training camp praise should always be taken with some caution. Pads have only recently come on, and real football is still weeks away. Still, when one of the team’s most respected veterans is repeatedly talking about the difference a newcomer has made after only a few practices, it’s worth paying attention. The Bengals didn’t trade for Dexter Lawrence simply to improve their defensive line on paper. They brought him in to raise the standard throughout the entire roster. If Ted Karras’ comments are any indication, that process is already well underway.

title: The time is now for DJ Ivey to prove he belongs
summary: After overcoming a devastating knee injury, Cincinnati Bengals cornerback DJ Ivey enters the biggest season of his NFL career with an opportunity to earn a permanent role in the secondary. DJ Ivey Cap Status Ivey is entering the final season of his four-year rookie contract after the Bengals selected him in the seventh round (246th overall) of […]
full_text: After overcoming a devastating knee injury, Cincinnati Bengals cornerback DJ Ivey enters the biggest season of his NFL career with an opportunity to earn a permanent role in the secondary. DJ Ivey Height: 6-foot-1 Weight: 192 pounds Age: 26 College: Miami (FL) Hometown: Homestead, Florida Experience: 3 years Cap Status Ivey is entering the final season of his four-year rookie contract after the Bengals selected him in the seventh round (246th overall) of the 2023 NFL Draft. He is scheduled to earn a base salary of $1.145 million while carrying a cap hit of approximately $1.17 million. He will become an unrestricted free agent following the 2026 season. Background Seventh-round draft picks rarely enjoy long NFL careers. Many never make a 53-man roster. Ivey has already beaten those odds. A five-year starter at Miami, Ivey entered the NFL with the size, length, and athleticism teams covet in an outside cornerback. The Bengals believed he was worth developing, and he rewarded that faith by making the roster as a rookie. Unfortunately, just as his role began to expand during the 2023 season, Ivey suffered a torn ACL that ended his rookie campaign and forced him to spend much of the following year working his way back to full strength. Rather than allowing the injury to define him, though, Ivey quietly continued developing. He appeared in every game during the 2025 season, providing valuable depth in the secondary while becoming an important contributor on special teams. Although he played only limited defensive snaps, he finished the year with 12 tackles and three passes defended, showing encouraging progress whenever his number was called. Outlook on the 2026 Season and Beyond Cornerback may be one of the deepest positions on Cincinnati’s roster, but that doesn’t mean opportunities won’t come. In today’s NFL, injuries are inevitable, and teams often rely on four, five, or even six cornerbacks over the course of a season. When an opportunity arrives, the Bengals need someone they can count on. That is where Ivey comes in. While he has already proven he can overcome adversity, now he must prove he can become more than just quality depth. The Bengals have invested heavily in rebuilding their defense, and competition throughout the secondary will be fierce. If Ivey continues the steady development he has shown since returning from injury, he has every opportunity to carve out a meaningful defensive role while remaining one of the club’s most valuable special teams players. But with guys like Ceyair Wright, Bralyn Lux, and Ja’Sir Taylor also vying for roster spots, Ivey needs a good showing in camp and the preseason just to ensure he keeps his spot on the Bengals’ 53-man roster. In many ways, the NFL and NBA are alike in that way, as Cleveland Browns owner Jimmy Haslam is finding out . Last week, the Browns had a surprising visitor to training camp in Berea : DE Jadeveon Clowney . Many were shocked that Clowney and Cleveland were even on speaking terms after his comments about the team and DE Myles Garrett when he departed in 2022. Clowney has had a bit of a resurgence as a pass rusher, which would have helped offset the loss of Garrett after he was traded to the Los Angeles Rams. Clowney has compiled 24.5 sacks in the three seasons since leaving the Browns, but decided on Sunday that a reunion in Cleveland was not as tempting as a reunion with the Houston Texans, the team that selected him first overall in the 2014 NFL draft: Back to where it began for Jadeveon Clowney: The former No. 1 overall pick of the #Texans has agreed to terms with Houston, sources tell me and @RapSheet . title: Browns QB battle: What if Watson or Sanders are not the best options?
summary: The Cleveland Browns are just four days into their latest, but far from greatest, quarterback training camp battle with no clear winner at the moment. That is not completely unsurprising for those who have been following along as first-time head coach Todd Monken has to choose between a broken and ineffective quarterback whose last good […]
full_text: BEREA, OHIO - JUNE 11: Shedeur Sanders #2 of the Cleveland Browns laughs with Deshaun Watson #4 during the Cleveland Browns Mandatory Minicamp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on June 11, 2026 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images The Cleveland Browns are just four days into their latest, but far from greatest, quarterback training camp battle with no clear winner at the moment. That is not completely unsurprising for those who have been following along as first-time head coach Todd Monken has to choose between a broken and ineffective quarterback whose last good season came in 2020, and a former fifth-round draft pick who posted one of the worst rookie seasons in the past 25 years. Monken is drawing out the decision as long as he possibly can , or, perhaps more accurately, delaying the public announcement until the team has a few more practices to confirm what he has already determined to be the correct course of action. It may still be a while until Monken announces who the starter will be, as he explained on Saturday : “I don’t think you’re really going to know until you get through all the installs, because we’re not game planning against our own defense. Each day has been a different part of the pass game, so it’s hard to really [tell]. And one day you go with the ones, the other day you go with the twos; certainly that matchup is going to be different depending on who you’re going against. “I think the most important thing is, from a process standpoint, how are we operating at the line of scrimmage, where are their eyes, have they taken command of the huddle, and then cadence, and then understanding the concepts. I think they’re all doing well; they’re all fine. All of our players are working through mistakes and fighting like hell to get better.” On the one hand, it would be nice if Monken just announced a decision and everyone could move on to preparing for the season opener in Jacksonville. On the other hand, neither Deshaun Watson nor Shedeur Sanders is likely to be the answer beyond this season, so what is a few more days or weeks of waiting really going to hurt? The fans and media are not the only ones watching the competition, of course, as the rest of the team is keeping tabs on what is happening on the practice field and forming their own opinions on what the right call would be. And the “word in the locker room” is that the best quarterback on the Browns right now is not named Watson or Sanders. That is according to Breiden Fehoko, a former defensive lineman who played three years in the NFL with the Los Angeles Chargers and is now host of The Fehoko Show on X: Don’t shoot the messenger. Word in the Cleveland Browns locker room is the best quarterback isn’t Deshaun or Shedeur right now……👀 — Breiden Fehoko (@BreidenFehoko) August 2, 2026 Fehoko does not reveal who dropped that word in his ear or who the locker room believes is the best quarterback at the moment. The only other choices are Taylen Green, a rookie sixth-round draft choice, or Dillon Gabriel, a second-year quarterback who just so happens to share a home state with Fehoko. The Browns are off today and will have their first practice in pads on Monday, providing Monken with more to consider as he ponders the starting quarterback for the season. Whether or not his choice aligns with the locker room or Fehoko’s personal choice remains to be seen.

title: Browns history: A rare Paul Warfield interview, catching up with the 1964 champion
summary: If there is a single athlete who can be pointed out as having an excellent athletic career, it has to be receiver Paul Warfield. He has three professional football championship rings with two different teams. Warfield was a college national champion. A track champion. Played for numerous exceptional head coaches. Was drafted by his childhood […]
full_text: UNITED STATES - NOVEMBER 08: Football: Closeup of Cleveland Browns Paul Warfield (42) before game vs Washington Redskins, Washington, DC 11/8/1964 (Photo by Tony Tomsic/Sports Illustrated via Getty Images) (SetNumber: X10387 Tk3 F5) If there is a single athlete who can be pointed out as having an excellent athletic career, it has to be receiver Paul Warfield. He has three professional football championship rings with two different teams. Warfield was a college national champion. A track champion. Played for numerous exceptional head coaches. Was drafted by his childhood team in the first round. Is a roster member of the NFL’s only unbeaten and untied squad. Has been inducted into six different Halls of Fame. Became a member of the largest sports contract ever. An All-American. Named to the NFL 100th Anniversary Team. And he was a first-ballot Pro Football Hall of Fame inductee. RELATED: GARY COLLINS INTERVIEW: 1964 NFL CHAMPS MVP Paul Warfield also bled orange. Sometimes it was for the Miami Dolphins, but mostly, it was because of the Cleveland Browns. His childhood home was in Warren, Ohio, just a little over an hour drive southeast of Cleveland. Warfield grew up loving the Cleveland Indians and the Cleveland Browns. And he still does, despite being 83 years old. Warfield attended Warren Harding High School, and sports kept him busy. He played basketball, baseball, and football, but was a star on the track team. He was a champion of the low hurdles, high jump, and one of the nation’s best broad jumpers. With this, he had Olympic aspirations. He had his hopes on becoming a professional baseball player as a catcher. But what swayed him to football was the fact that many baseball players lingered in the minor league system. And some really great high school players remained in the minors for years and years. Warfield did not want to chance this and decided to focus on football. He also wanted an opportunity to pursue track in college. Paul Warfield’s accolades in college: National champion ( 1961 ) First-team All-American ( 1963 ) Two-time First-team All-Big Ten ( 1962 , 1963 ) Ohio State Varsity O Hall of Fame (1979) Warfield had his choice of colleges after playing running back and defensive back in high school. His choice came down to Ohio State University and the University of Iowa. In the end, he decided to remain close to home and stay in Ohio. He was drafted by the Browns with the #11 pick in Round 1 of the 1964 NFL draft. He was also selected in the fourth round of the American Football League (AFL) draft by the Buffalo Bills. The 1964 Bills would go on to win their first AFL championship. In Warfield’s first year with the Browns, he began as a defensive back, but head coach Blanton Collier switched him to receiver. Notice that Warfield wore #42. That is a running back and defensive back’s number. Back then, receivers wore digits in the 80s. That 1964 season culminated with Cleveland defeating the league’s best ballclub, the high-scoring Baltimore Colts 27-0 in the 1964 “NFL Championship Game.” In 1969, Browns GM Harold Sauerbrei traded Warfield to the Miami Dolphins for the third overall pick in the 1970 NFL draft. That was the first year that all 10 AFL teams would merge into the NFL. The Browns had lost the 1969 “NFL Championship Game” and were picking at the bottom of the first round. They wanted to get Purdue QB Mike Phipps and needed to get into the Top-5. Don Shula had just been named the new head coach of the Dolphins, an AFL expansion club. Miami would go on to go to three consecutive Super Bowls, winning two, including the 1972 perfect season going 17-0-0. Warfield played 13 years in the NFL and one in the World Football League (WFL). The breakdown is six years with the Browns, followed by five with Miami, in which the Dolphins went to three Super Bowls and won two. He then spent half a year with the Memphis Southmen of the WFL, and finally two seasons back in Cleveland. In his eight years with Cleveland, he had 271 receptions for 5,210 yards and 52 touchdowns. What was his running style? Poetry in motion. Paul Warfield’s accolades in the pros: NFL champion ( 1964 ) Two-time Super Bowl champion ( VII , VIII ) Two-time First-team All-Pro ( 1971 , 1973 ) Three-time Second-team All-Pro ( 1968 , 1970 , 1972 ) Eight-time Pro Bowl ( 1964 , 1968 – 1974 ) Two-time NFL receiving touchdowns leader (1968, 1971) Warfield’s league and team accolades: Cleveland Browns Ring of Honor Miami Dolphins Honor Roll Dolphins Walk of Fame (2011) NFL 1970s All-Decade Team NFL 100th Anniversary All-Time Team Pro Football Hall of Fame (1983) Florida Sports Hall of Fame (1992) In 1977, Warfield earned a master’s degree in telecommunications from Kent State University. After he hung up his cleats, he worked for WKYC in Cleveland as a sportscaster from 1977 to 1980. Then, from 1981 to 1987, he worked as director of player relations for the Browns. Later, he was senior adviser to the general manager for the team. A life-size statue of Warfield was erected in 2013 outside the stadium at Warren Harding High School, with the label “Pride of Warren, Ohio.” They inducted him into their Warren Sports Hall of Fame in 1989. Today, Warfield is officially retired and still has ties to the State of Ohio, but lives just east of Los Angeles. Dawgs by Nature staff writer Barry Shuck was able to catch up with Warfield to discuss that magical 1964 NFL season, where, as a rookie, Cleveland became NFL champions. Shuck: While playing for Warren Harding High School, you played basketball and were a defensive back and a running back in football. You were a high jump champion and the broad jump champion, as well as a 180-yard low hurdles state champion. If you could relive any race you have done in the past, which one would it be? Warfield: I was competing in what they called low hurdles and became the State Champion. I also competed in the 100-yard dash and the broad jump, in which I placed third in the State. I guess the one race that stands out was the final race I ran in the low hurdles, which was also my final race in scholastic competition, in the colors of Warren Harding High School. It was for the Ohio State Champion meet. I won the race and set a new state record at 18.9. Our school almost won the state championship but was a few points short. Shuck: You played under the legendary Woody Hayes at Ohio State. What type of coach was he? And did you pick OSU because they would allow you to participate in track also? Warfield: Coach Hayes was a great coach. I was recruited by quite a number of schools, and my decision boiled down to whether to attend a Big 10 conference school. My decision boiled down to Ohio State and also the University of Iowa. I chose, as a scholastic athlete, to remain in the State of Ohio. We analyzed the university so that I could continue my education, and I went around the university with my visit with the aides. Coach Hayes was a great, great coach, certainly. He knew football, and it was a great experience for me. And he had a format that he really stressed education for all of the athletes who were in the school. All of the schools that I talked to about attending knew I wanted to participate in track and field. So, I listened to the ones that were acceptable to that, like the University of Iowa. Shuck: At one time, you had Olympic aspirations in track. Why did this change? Warfield: Possibly because it was not going to be an Olympic year. The 1964 Summer Olympics were next, and I graduated that year. Basically, I had a decision to make. That competition comes once every four years, and I was drafted by the Cleveland Browns at the same time. I would have loved to have an opportunity to be a part of the United States track and field team, but what had more weight at the same time was that I was eligible to play professional football. Shuck: In 1961, Ohio State finished 8-0-1, and Alabama ended its season 11-0-0. Two services named OSU National…

(Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images The Cleveland Browns have a lot of new bodies in training camp this year. Besides the usual signings of undrafted rookie free agents, many starters from last year’s roster have retired, been released, or just weren’t offered a new deal going into 2026. This year’s rookies appear to be another winning class for GM Andrew Berry. We will see. Which ones will become starters? Can these new guys help on game day, or are they more developmental at this stage? RELATED: WHICH BROWNS’ ROOKIE WILL HAVE THE BEST YEAR – PART 1 Here at Dawgs by Nature, we asked several Browns experts to pick a rookie player and then describe why they thought that new guy could become the best of his class. For this upcoming season, when it’s all said and done, which player will be this year’s best rookie? EZ Weav DBN Staff S Emmanuel McNeil-Warren It’s hard to qualify this question; in a general sense, expectations of rookies should be fairly low, but everybody is out of patience, and so nobody will get any grace. Thus, how one does is going to be contingent on what the expectations are of them, and for better or worse. Spencer Fano, KC Concepcion, and Denzel Boston all will not only have higher expectations (probably) than what is reasonable. But also, a large part of their success is going to be determined pretty directly by the quality of the QB play, and in case you haven’t noticed, ours is not exactly the strongest room in the league. Thus, I’ll go with safety Emmanuel McNeil-Warren. He’s going to have a lot less pressure on him to perform, and he doesn’t need as many things to go right for him to be successful as the offensive guys will need. And he’s going into a room with solid starters already, from whom he can gain some good tutelage. Throw in that the fans (and broadcasters, media, and pretty much everyone other than the players and the coaches) don’t see about 95% of what safeties actually ever even do, so as long as he’s not an obvious liability (like rookie-year Jabrill Peppers), he’s got the most talent/easiest road combo. Glenn Bam Caudill Wayne County Browns Backers – Wooster, Ohio WR Denzel Boston I think Denzel Boston will have a good year. At 6’-4”, 212 pounds, the wide receiver from the Washington Huskies has the body type and great hands to win the contested catches. The Huskies’ lack of receiving threats led to him seeing double teams at the college level frequently. He was selected by our Browns at 39th overall in the second round of the 2026 NFL Draft. Most pre-draft experts considered him a first-round pick while Pro Football Focus listed him a few spots ahead of receiver KC Concepcion. Playing 25 games in the last two years, he had over 120 catches, 1,700 yards, and 20 touchdowns. This plays into a move-the-chains and score in the red zone on a consistent basis weapon, which we sorely need. With legitimate receiving threats on the field with him, he will have good chances to make damage on the defense. The preseason hype started early for him in the practices this spring as he looked the part of the big-bodied WR this team has been needing. I predict that he surpasses Cedric Tillman to win a starting job by game one, and he will lead the team in TDs this year with 10. Angeline Adams Administrator: Cleveland Browns We Bark Together LINK: CLEVELAND BROWNS WE BARK TOGETHER OT Spencer Fano Every “Good Dawg” knows that one of the most crucial elements in championship football is winning at the line of scrimmage. Elite left tackles are among the rarest and most valuable players in football, with some of the most difficult tasks of pivotal pass protection, relentless run blocking, and critical communication. To the delight of GM Andrew Berry and many diehard Browns fans, Browns rookie offensive tackle Spencer Fano is no newbie at top-tier dominating in the trenches and will lock in at left tackle. When the Browns selected Fano, the ninth overall pick, he already possessed one of the most premier profiles of any college football offensive linemen. At the University of Utah, he showcased unique toughness and superior versatility by excelling at both left and right tackles. Fano played 37 career games with 36 starts. His dominance was distinguished in his accolades, including team Captain, 2025 Outland Trophy Winner, Unanimous First Team Associated Press All-American, Big 12 “Offensive Lineman of the Year,” First Team All-Big 12 Honors, as well as “Polynesian College Football Player of the Year.” Before arriving in “The Land,” in his final and most masterful season as a Ute, Fano played 822 offensive snaps without surrendering a sack or allowing a quarterback hit. Skill players may electrify audiences with dazzling catches, explosive runs, or a pick-six, but a left tackle of Fano’s caliber proves his value on every offensive snap. As a matter of fact, if our quarterback or running back keeps getting slammed on his back from rushing attacks, there can be no flashy highlight reels for fans to catch. What separates Fano from every other Browns rookie is that his value extends far beyond individual statistics. His athleticism helps him mirror elite edge rushers, his footwork keeps him balanced in pass protection, and his strength opens running lanes that may never make the highlight reel but can decide games. With powerful hands and the versatility to thrive in both zone-and power-blocking schemes, he gives the offense a reliable foundation. Every successful pass, explosive run, and game-winning drive starts with protection in the trenches. That is Fano’s wheelhouse. Fano also excels in his football instincts. Coaches consistently praised his processing speed, preparation, discipline, leadership, and competitive toughness. Fano’s understanding of defensive schemes, blitz recognition, and pass protection allows him to anticipate defenders before the play unfolds, making him one of the most polished offensive tackle prospects in his draft class. Those traits tend to translate to the NFL more reliably than many athletic traits. Spencer Fano was my top graded offensive tackle (OT1) in the 2026 NFL Draft https://t.co/IYY1HpK6jm — FIRST ROUND MOCK (@firstroundmock) July 28, 2026 His weaknesses are surprisingly few. Some questioned whether his arm length is ideal for the position and noted that he can occasionally rely on athleticism instead of more forceful hand placement against elite speed rushers. The good news is that those are coachable corrections rather than fundamental flaws. It was his remarkable consistency, technical refinement, athletic traits, and football intelligence that elevated him into the Top-10 of the NFL Draft. Fano was selected to be foundational, a cornerstone of Cleveland’s offense – not to score touchdowns himself, but to create the protection and running lanes that allow everyone else to do just that. After six long months without football, the sight of those orange helmets, daily quarterback trackers, and hearing from the coaches and players about mostly meaningful topics is always welcome. Then there is the annual media day where ownership talks about expectations for the season and, to some extent, shares the overall feeling about the current state of the franchise.” Browns GM Andrew Berry refuses to follow Sashi Brown’s, other failed regimes’ processes (Jared Mueller) – “In many ways, Cleveland Browns GM Andrew Berry’s resume can be separated by what happened before the 2025 NFL draft (specifically the Deshaun Watson trade, which led to moving on from Baker Mayfield) and everything that has happened since the start of that draft. Before the 2025 draft, Berry made a lot of moves to try to open up and create a Super Bowl window for the Browns.” The Feed What do you think? Share your thoughts in Dawgs By Nature’s Feed in the comment section or by following this link to the Feed post . Cleveland Browns What has to stop right now as the Browns prepare for the season? (Terry Pluto) – “Will the Browns look like they “have their act together?” Browns owner Jimmy Haslam said that’s one of the goals for the 2026 season.” Shedeur Sanders, Deshaun Watson still figuring it out in Browns QB battle (Beacon Journal) – “Every throw has been chronicled. Every social media video has been broken down by thousands in order to gain some insight into who’s ahead. Turns out, for all of the talk about who’s leading between Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders for the Browns’ starting quarterback job, the person making the decision doesn’t really have a lean yet. In fact, coach Todd Monken would tell you that the evaluation process hasn’t even started.” How Shedeur Sanders is locked in on one thing this Browns camp and nothing else matters (cleveland.com) – “Shedeur Sanders had his game face on before Day 4 of Browns training camp on Saturday and didn’t break character throughout his 10-minute availability. He’s locked in on improving each day, and not even a visit from his ultra-famous father Deion Sanders was enough to distract him on Thursday.” Shedeur Sanders focused on improvement, not QB battle: ‘nothing matters to me if it is not helping us win’ (Browns Zone) – “Shedeur Sanders had his game face on well before practice started. “Nothing matters to me if it is not helping us win,” he said Saturday before Day 4 of training camp.” NFL Confident Will Levis OK competing for Titans’ backup QB spot (ESPN) – “Tennessee Titans quarterback Will Levis was all smiles when he spoke to the media for the first time since being placed on injured reserve last year before training camp. He was confident, too, and adamantly believes he’s “a dang good quarterback.” Levis is entering his fourth season but has a much different approach to football after being away from the game for a full season for the first time since second grade.” Ricky Pearsall waiting to have surgery on PCL wasn’t avoidance; it was medically sound (Niners Nation) – “Ricky Pearsall is currently out of the San Francisco 49ers’ training camp with a PCL injury, and initial reports say he might be out for much longer than that. title: Cowboys news: Trading for Jordyn Brooks is the rumor that won’t die
summary: Jordyn Brooks and the 1 Clue Everyone Missed – Cody Warren, Inside The Star It could make more sense than most believe. The Jordyn Brooks Connection Has Always Been There Dallas has already been connected to Jordyn Brooks, and Miami had several teams calling about him earlier this offseason. When I went back and looked at what […]
full_text: Jul 31, 2026; Miami Gardens, FL, USA; Miami Dolphins linebacker Jordyn Brooks (20) works during practice at Baptist Health Training Complex. Mandatory Credit: Sam Navarro-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Jordyn Brooks and the 1 Clue Everyone Missed – Cody Warren, Inside The Star It could make more sense than most believe. The Jordyn Brooks Connection Has Always Been There Dallas has already been connected to Jordyn Brooks , and Miami had several teams calling about him earlier this offseason. When I went back and looked at what Brooks did last year : 183 tackles, 13 tackles for loss, 3.5 sacks, and a first-team All-Pro nod in 2025. To say that is attention grabbing may be downplaying it. If Dallas somehow pulled this off, Brooks isn’t coming in to compete for snaps. He’s coming in to be the best player in the room. I thought the idea was dead when Miami signed him to a three-year, $51.3 million extension with $35 million guaranteed. My first reaction to this deal was pretty simple, “Well, there goes that player.” But then I dug into the contract more. According to Over The Cap, Jordyn Brooks got a $12.31 million signing bonus, while his 2026 base salary is only $1.215 million. Miami already paid the bonus and that changed the whole way I looked at this trade. The $51.3 million headline makes the deal sound impossible. Once I got past that number and looked at what Dallas would actually be dealing with in 2026, I didn’t brush it off. The Cowboys waived one of their free agent signees. The @dallascowboys made the following transactions on Sunday. Signed: OL Sebastian Gutierrez Waived/Injured: OLB Charles Snowden — Dallas Cowboys Public Relations (@DallasCowboysPR) August 2, 2026 Sam Williams is giving the Cowboys a problem they should gladly accept – Jerry Trotta, The Landry Hat Hopefully Williams adds depth to a position the Cowboys desperately need. So far, Williams is thriving under that pressure, as he’s been among a handful of defensive standouts over the first two practices of camp. He caught the eye of Cowboys team reporter Nick Eatman, who went as far as to say that Williams has looked “dominant.” “Sam Williams has a big opportunity in front of him this year and he looked rather dominant during the team drills,” Eatman wrote. “On two straight plays, he showed the variety of skill set the Cowboys have always admired from Williams, who ran stride for stride with running back Dominic Richardson on a wheel route down the field, and then stuffed the same running back in the hole on the next play. Also, Williams lived in the backfield, creating all kinds of pressure rushing from the left side.” This is exactly the kind of problem the Cowboys should welcome with open arms. A Sam Williams breakout would change the complexion of the Cowboys’ defense A lot will be asked of Rashan Gary and Donovan Ezeiruaku in the outside linebacker (EDGE) room. Gary’s run-defending chops give him a high floor, while Ezeiruaku’s untapped potential could determine just how dangerous this pass rush becomes. The Biggest Mistake Dallas Cowboys Can’t Afford to Make This Training Camp – Zach Dimmitt, Sports Illustrated Dallas needs to be uncharacteristically aggressive this offseason. Dallas can’t afford to overlook any opportunities to improve the defense , even if that means making a move during training camp. Any sort of shortcoming the coaching staff can pinpoint on that side of the ball shouldn’t be taken with a grain of salt. The Cowboys know that the defense can’t risk starting out the season on the wrong note, or it could lead to a similar result last year where Dallas found itself chasing a playoff spot before it was too late. Instead of waiting until the trade deadline like last season when they landed defensive tackle Quinnen Williams from the New York Jets, it might benefit the Cowboys to stop a bleeding noise before it gets too messy. Many fans will point to a potential blockbuster deal with the Las Vegas Raiders for star edge rusher Maxx Crosby as a move that Dallas can’t risk passing up, but the Cowboys could be better off making a move in the secondary if the new additions of Cobie Durant, Jalen Thompson and PJ Locke don’t work out as the front office had hoped, or worse, injuries start to pile up in the back end. Cowboys fans also have their concerns about the output from safety Malik Hooker and cornerback DaRon Bland. Though Bland has historical production on his resume, making him the feature piece of a big trade can’t be ruled out, even with the four-year, $90 million contract extension he signed last August. 4 Cowboys miss Saturday’s camp practice include 2x Pro Bowl starter – Angel Torres, Cowboys Wire Nothing to be concerned with yet, just worth monitoring. Safeties P.J. Locke and Jalen Thompson, both offseason free-agent acquisitions , will miss the team’s third practice of training camp. Cornerback Zion Childress will also be held out with an injury of his own. Locke seemed to hyperextend his knee on the first day of on-field work and although the team deemed it minor, he will miss his second-straight practice. Thompson, according to head coach Brian Schottenheimer, was sidelined with a bothersome hip. Childress has a hamstring issue; the second-year corner has an uphill battle to earn a roster spot so every missed opportunity is concerning. Starting tight end Jake Ferguson will miss the practice due to personal reasons. Ferguson’s absence gave reserve TE Brevyn Spann-Ford, primed for a larger role , and the rest of the position group extra reps with the starting offense. Daily discussion question: Which new Cowboys player are you most excited about right now?
