title: Discussion: Which linebackers will make the Detroit Lions 53-man roster?
summary: The Detroit Lions’ linebacker group has quietly turned into a logjam. Between making an impact on defense and an impact on special teams, the Lions’ coaching staff will have some difficult decisions to make when roster cuts roll around. The Lions are lucky to have one of the league’s best in Jack Campbell, but the […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 4: Trevor Nowaske #53 of the Detroit Lions lines up during the first half of the NFL football game against the Chicago Bears at Solider Field on January 4, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions’ linebacker group has quietly turned into a logjam. Between making an impact on defense and an impact on special teams, the Lions’ coaching staff will have some difficult decisions to make when roster cuts roll around. The Lions are lucky to have one of the league’s best in Jack Campbell, but the rest of the depth chart has a lot to prove. Can Derrick Barnes have a rebound season to justify his expensive contract extension? Can Malcolm Rodriguez show that a subpar 2025 campaign was just rust from a prior ACL injury? Which of their depth players can stake a claim on a coveted roster spot? With more training camp and preseason still to come, we can hope for some clarity, but we could just as easily be left with a tough decision: whom to keep and whom to cut? Today’s Question of the Day is: Which linebackers will make the Detroit Lions 53-man roster? My answer: My current guess is six: Jack Campbell, Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, Damone Clark, Trevor Nowaske, and Troy Reeder. The first three names on that list are obvious and require no explanation. The back half of the linebacker room is where the discussion starts. In the past, the Lions have liked to keep six linebackers in total. In 2025, the team kept six linebackers despite an initial roster of just 50 players. The same can be said about 2024 and 2023—that is three seasons in a row with six linebackers on the Week 1 roster. We can use 2025 as a template for what the Lions like: they have typically kept three starting-caliber players (Campbell, Barnes, and Alex Anzalone), one backup with defensive capabilities (Zach Cunningham), and two backups with special teams roles (Grant Stuard and Nowaske). As it stands, the Lions currently have 10 linebackers on the 90-man roster and you could make a genuine case for all of them. Starting trio of Campbell, Barnes, and Rodriguez aside, you have rookie Jimmy Rolder, a player that would undoubtedly be a roster lock if not for an injury with an as-of-yet unknown timeline . Then there is Clark, a veteran with a mix of defensive experience, special teams experience, and youth. Trevor Nowaske returns for yet another season in Detroit as a player that has grown into a valued special teamer with SAM potential on defense. These three are my favorite bubble players to make the roster, pending Rolder’s injury status. Joining the group are three veterans in Devin White, Joe Bachie, and Reeder. White is the newest of the signings and is coming off a 174-tackle season, albeit to poor performance grades . Bachie has bounced around the league, starting the occasional game but largely being a special teams contributor. Reeder, meanwhile, had been a frequent starter for the Los Angeles Rams since 2019, but 2025 was the first year in which he was largely relegated to special teams duties. Rounding out the linebacker room is undrafted rookie Erick Hunter, a player with an intriguing athletic profile and a strong developmental ceiling. Because Rolder’s status is presently up in the air and it prompted the Lions to sign White immediately, I think there is a decent chance he starts the season on the Injured Reserve. This would cause him to miss at least four games, an unfortunate circumstance but not a career-altering one. Odds are the Lions will not need Rolder in the early part of the season, especially if he is unable to play during training camp and preseason. That leaves me at five linebackers (Campbell, Barnes, Rodriguez, Clark, and Nowaske) and despite the Lions shifting away from three-linebacker sets, I still think they will want to keep six. I give my early nod to Reeder. Because Clark could realistically be a solid LB4 on defense and a solid contributor on special teams, I think the value of keeping a defense-only option like White is greatly reduced. That increases the value of Reeder, who could step into a role on defense or special teams when called upon. It is also worth remembering that the Lions only signed White after Rolder’s injury, whereas Reeder was signed at the start of training camp—sure, this is only a difference of a few days, but White’s signing was reactionary, while Reeder’s was not, perhaps hinting at Reeder being a more coveted option. How will the Lions’ crowded linebacker room shake out? Let us know in the comments below.
author: John Whiticar

title: Devin White explains why he signed with the Detroit Lions
summary: Devin White has pretty much always seen success wherever he’s gone. LSU posted a 27-11 record during his time in college. He won a Super Bowl in the second year of his NFL career. He’s made the playoffs in five of his seven season in the pros. But last year with the Las Vegas Raiders […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - DECEMBER 7: Devin White #45 of the Las Vegas Raiders stretches on the field prior to an NFL football game against the Denver Broncos at Allegiant Stadium on December 07, 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Devin White has pretty much always seen success wherever he’s gone. LSU posted a 27-11 record during his time in college. He won a Super Bowl in the second year of his NFL career. He’s made the playoffs in five of his seven season in the pros. But last year with the Las Vegas Raiders was different. As a 17-game starter, White watched the Raiders quickly fall out of contention. The team fell apart and finished a 3-14. “Coming off last year, losing season, that was like the first time ever (for me),” White said. “I ain’t never lost or having a losing season in my career since I was a kid, so that was very hard.” [Editor’s note: He did go through a 7-9 and 8-9 season with the Buccaneers.] This offseason, he made sure that wasn’t going to happen again. He had some offers that came in early in free agency. After all, we’re talking about former fifth overall pick, a Pro Bowler, and a player who finished last season with 17 starts and finished third in the NFL in tackles. But White wasn’t interested in going to the highest bigger or the most eager team. He was going to be selective and patient with his process. “I feel like just jumping out there head first and putting myself back in the position I was in last year–a lot of other teams, they’re probably a lot of pieces away from getting to even the postseason, and I really didn’t want to deal with that,” White siad. “I want to go in and be able to help a team that really wants to win right now.” White said he had contact with the Lions early in the free agent process, but put plans on the shelf. Then on Friday, Lions linebacker Jimmy Rolder suffered an injury that’s expected to keep him out a while. Detroit had White on a flight to Detroit that night. White was immediately drawn to Detroit’s ability to compete for a title, but when he arrived, he was only more impressed. The culture lived up to its reputation, particularly because of all the coaches around who played in this league before. “I think this was the right fit for me being around some ball-coaches who actually played the game, can actually get out there, hands on with you, and let’s keep improving,” White said. “Let’s keep improving whatever they think I can improve in, they can actually get out there and coach me , coach me, because they did it before. So they know exactly what they’re looking for.” It may take some time for White to acclimate and climb the depth chart. While he spent the offseason making sure he was physically and mentally ready to jump back in at a moment’s notice, he now has a new playbook to learn. And while the coverages are all familiar, the terminology is not. Still, White is proud of the work he put in during Sunday’s practice—his first with Detroit—and he’s ready to take things to a new level when the pads come on Monday. “I just finished Day 1 of practice, and it was a good one,” White said. “I gotta go back and get back into film study so I can come back tomorrow with the pads on and be a lot faster and a lot more physical. So I’ll be trying to get acclimated to that.”

title: Lions training camp Day 4 observations: Defense clamps in red zone
summary: The rain managed to stay away for Day 4 of Detroit Lions training camp, but the field was still relatively slippery out there. Nevertheless, the Lions were able to get a full day’s worth of work in, and plenty of team drills to draw upon for observations. Here’s what we learned from Sunday’s practice. Note: […]
full_text: Detroit Lions cornerback D.J. Reed (4) practices during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Thursday, July 30, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The rain managed to stay away for Day 4 of Detroit Lions training camp, but the field was still relatively slippery out there. Nevertheless, the Lions were able to get a full day’s worth of work in, and plenty of team drills to draw upon for observations. Here’s what we learned from Sunday’s practice. Note : If you want a full injury/participation breakdown of Sunday’s practice, you can find that here . Miles Frazier is everywhere With Giovanni Manu and Ben Bartch out, and Blake Miller limited to individual drills, the Lions needed Miles Frazier to play just about every position… and he did. I would say the majority of his reps came at tackle—and he got some significant work as the starting right tackle—but he also got time at both guard positions. While it would certainly benefit him most to focus in on the left guard position, where the starting job is up for grabs, he is clearly showcasing his versatility, and he had an overall very strong day on Sunday (more on that later). 1-on-1 WR vs. DBs winners and losers Winners Every Amon-Ra St. Brown vs. D.J. Reed rep This is becoming must-see TV as the two players are at the top of their game. On the first rep, it looked like Reed was all over St. Brown, but a perfectly placed ball from Jared Goff and some late hands from St. Brown resulted in an improbable catch. Thomas Harper This expands beyond 1-on-1s, but Harper—who has had a quiet start to camp—had two forced incompletions during 1-on-1s against Malik Cunningham and Lawrence Keys. During red zone 7-on-7s, he also perfectly timed a pass from Teddy Bridgewater for the interception, but landed out of the back of the end zone. Dominic Lovett I’ve been hard on Lovett, but he came down with two big wins during 1-on-1s: he had an incredible one-handed back-shoulder grab opposite Keith Abney, then toasted De’Shawn Rucker off his release for an easy grab. Lucky Jackson The former UFL receiver had two very impressive reps, and both were against potential starters. The first, he cleanly beat McCreary with an impressive, slippery release for a wide-open touchdown grab. The second, he probably got away with a push-off, but showed some physicality by creating separation on Rock Ya-Sin. Losers Isaac TeSlaa It’s been a slow start to camp from TeSlaa, but this may have been his worst day of practice. He went 0-for-5 during 1-on-1s and was particularly struggling against press corners. Rock Ya-Sin, Roger McCreary, and Avonte Maddox all posted wins against the second-year receiver More 1-on-1 OL/DL winners and losers Note: I was watching DB/WR drills during this portion of this practice, so the following observations are from our own Al Karsten: Below are the combined win-loss-tie records for each offensive lineman against the defensive line over two separate sessions. The defense controlled the opening period before the offense responded with a vengeance, winning the majority of the second session. A few notes: Blake Miller did not participate in the one-on-ones, while several first-team veterans—including Aidan Hutchinson and Penei Sewell—only took a limited number of reps. As an added bonus, assistant coach Dan Skipper served as the de facto quarterback throughout both drills. Keep in mind these periods move extremely fast, and some reps are close calls when determining whether the pass rusher or offensive lineman earned the win. Devin Cochran (LT) — 3-2-0 vs. Tyler Lacy (1-0), Eric O’Neill (1-1), Anthony Lucas (0-2) Lacy got him on an impressive outside swim move to seal off Cochran around the corner O’Neill showed off a nice little burst to get outside on the first rep, but Cochran swallowed him on the second rep Juice Scruggs (LG) — 1-2-0 vs. Levi Onwuzurike (1-0), Alim McNeill (1-0), Tyler Lacy (0-1) Onwuzurike walked Scruggs back into the QB McNeill also powered Scruggs into the backfield Cade Mays (C) — 2-1-0 vs. Tyleik Williams (1-1), Myles Adams (0-1) Williams had a really good first step penetration, but Mays did recover well in a close-fought battle. Mays had really solid positioning on the second rep Mays swallowed Adams whole Tate Ratledge (RG) — 2-0-1 vs. Alim McNeill (0-1), Levi Onwuzurike (0-0-1), Mekhi Wingo (0-1) McNeill got stonewalled in a great rep by Ratledge Ratledge and Onwuzurike had a physical rep that we’ll call a draw with Ratledge second reaction recovery Larry Borom (RT, LT) — 4-0-0 vs. DJ Wonnum (0-2), Ahmed Hassanein (0-1), Derrick Moore (0-1) Borom anchored on a bull rush the first rep against Wonnum, then a second rep sat on a spin move inside Borom kept Moore shielded off outside on a swim counter move Miles Frazier (LG, RT, LT) — 7-1-0 vs. Skyler Gill-Howard (0-2), Anthony Lucas (0-2), Derrick Moore (1-1), Ahmed Hassanein (0-1), Eric O’Neill (0-1) Checked Gill-Howard up right at the line of scrimmage Moore attempted a Hutchinson-esque set-up to go outside-inside with a spin move, and Frazier clobbered him to the ground. On their second rep, Moore got Frazier on an outside rip Hassanein worked to set up a second counter move, and Frazier didn’t take the bait Christian Mahogany (LG) — 3-0-0 vs. Myles Adams (0-1), Alim McNeill (0-1), Mekhi Wingo (0-1) Mahogany rode Adams out of the pocket after initially losing ground In the most impressive individual rep of one-on-one pass rush drills, Mahogany dominated McNeill and had him flailing with his back to the quarterback, eating on a McNeill spin move Mahogany definitively sat on an inside swim move from Wingo Penei Sewell (LT) — 0-1 vs. Aidan Hutchinson (1-0) In their only reps, Hutchinson won on the outside with a swim but slipped turning the corner Colby Sorsdal (RT, RG) — 1-2-0 vs. Derrick Moore (1-0), Ahmed Hassanein (1-0), Tyre West (0-1) Moore got a decisive win on the outside Hassanein was a train on the tracks and had a good bull rush Mason Miller (RG, RT) — 3-2-0 vs. Mekhi Wingo (0-1), Skyler Gill-Howard (1-1), Tyre West (0-1), Derrick Moore (1-0) Wingo got an initial push, but Miller surprised powerfully on a second effort to shut it down Gill-Howard looked like his Texas Tech self with a nice swim inside on the first rep, with the second rep going as a tie and a potentially questionable Miller hold Miller beat West with West shoving him in the back after causing a small scuffle Moore beat Miller, at RT, on an outside dip Seth McLaughlin (C) — 4-1-0 vs. Chris Smith (1-1), Aidan Keanaaina (0-2), Myles Adams (0-1) After an initial slip, McLaughlin sturdily regained his anchor against Smith. On their next rep against each other, Smith won with a bull rush. Melvin Priestly (RG) — 2-0-2 vs. Tyre West (0-0-1), Myles Adams (0-0-1), Skyler Gill-Howard (0-2) West tried an inside hump move, which gained ground initially before Priestly recollected himself in the pocket Michael Niese (C) — 2-0-2 vs. Aidan Keanaaina (0-1-1), Tyler Lacy (0-1), Tyre West (0-0-1) Defense dominates in the red zone Once we moved to team play, the defense was absolutely dominant in the red zone, led by some strong play from the linebackers. The first series (7-on-7s), Malcolm Rodriguez broke up an attempted Texas route to Sione Vaki with perfect coverage. Then a few plays later, Jameson Williams bobbled a ball only for it to go right into the hands of Reed for the interception. The first-team offense did manage to find the end zone once with a pick-play concept that got TeSlaa open for the short touchdown grab. When we moved to 11-on-11s, everyone on defense was getting into the mix. Ya-Sin continued his strong day with a pass breakup opposite TeSlaa. Tyleik Williams and D.J. Reed picked up tackles for loss in the run game. And Jack Campbell immediately scurried through traffic to find Vaki after a dump-off from Goff. When the first-team came back after that failed series, it was all about the linebackers. Campbell tallied another stop…

title: Detroit Lions training camp injury report: Good news on Alim McNeill, Christian Izien
summary: With the Detroit Lions taking the field for Day 4 of training camp on Sunday, it was another opportunity to get some updates on the health of their players. For the most part, it was good news—particularly when it comes to Alim McNeill and Christian Izien. The news is a little more mixed for Jimmy […]
full_text: Aug 2, 2026; Allen Park, MI, USA; Detroit Lions defensive lineman Alim McNeill (54) looks on during Detroit Lions training camp at Meijer Performance Center. Mandatory Credit: Paul Barnick-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect With the Detroit Lions taking the field for Day 4 of training camp on Sunday, it was another opportunity to get some updates on the health of their players. For the most part, it was good news—particularly when it comes to Alim McNeill and Christian Izien. The news is a little more mixed for Jimmy Rolder and a few other players. Let’s break it all down below. Returned to practice: DT Alim McNeill (neck) S Christian Izien (NFI, flu) After leaving Friday’s practice early, McNeill was back on the field the next practice. He explained after practice that he had been kicked in the head on Friday and needed to go through evaluations. He’s fine. As expected, Izien made his training camp debut on Sunday. After battling the flu to start camp, he is officially off the Non-Football Illness list and got some work with the first and second teams at both nickel and safety Not practicing: RB Jahmyr Gibbs ( not-injury related ) TE Tyler Conklin (PUP, calf) OT Giovanni Manu (NFI) G Ben Bartch (unknown) EDGE Payton Turner (back) LB Jimmy Rolder (leg) S Kerby Joseph (PUP, knee) S Brian Branch (PUP, Achilles) It’s worth noting Jahmyr Gibbs was out on the field supporting his team as he continues his hold-in. This was the first time I’ve seen him out there with the team, but he avoided media after practice. Tyler Conklin looks to be on the path toward returning, as he spent nearly all of practice working with a trainer in some high-intensity drills. Typically, players get a week or so of on-field work before returning to practice, so don’t be surprised if it’s still another handful of practices before he re-enters the lineup. Bartch has yet to get involved in any team drills as Detroit eases him back from a 2025 injury, but on Sunday, he was only on the field briefly to get work with a trainer. Juice Scruggs took most of the first-team reps at left guard. Rolder is expected to miss some time with the leg injury suffered in Friday’s practice. There were mixed reports on the severity of his injury , but it’s worth noting that defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard said he believes Rolder will contribute this season. “I absolutely see him contributing at some point,” Sheppard said. Appeared to be limited RT Blake Miller (unknown) Miller went through walkthroughs and individual drills, but he did not take any full-team reps and was not participating in 1-on-1s. At this point, it isn’t clear if that’s scheduled rest or Detroit being precautionary. Larry Borom and Miles Frazier split time at right tackle with the first-team offense for most of practice. Left practice early TE Milles Kitselman (leg) EDGE Derrick Moore (groin) The Lions provided official updates on both players after practice, simply saying they were being evaluated for injury after practice. I did not personally witness the injuries nor their exit from the field.

full_text: Detroit Lions defensive lineman Aidan Keanaaina (60) practices during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co We’re only three practices into 2026 Detroit Lions training camp, but I can already get a sense that some of y’all are champing at the bit for more coverage. And with 90-ish people on the roster, there are still plenty of players to talk to, talk about, and analyze their play on the field. There will be plenty of opportunities to expand our coverage over the next few months. Not only are there approximately 16 more training camp practices ahead, but there are also three preseason games ahead. Our notebooks should be filled by the time we get to September. But, for now, I want to hear from y’all on our training camp coverage. Today’s Question of the Day is: Which Lions player do you want to hear more about at training camp? My answer: I’m going to try to take a closer look at Detroit’s pair of rookie interior defensive linemen: sixth-round pick Skyler Gill-Howard and seventh-round Tyre West. Admittedly, it’s been tough to get much of a read on either player thus far. For one, both players are regularly repping with the third and fourth string teams this early in cap (as expected). That limits the amount of reps they get each practice. Additionally, interior defensive line play is extremely hard to evaluate live with no replays. There’s a lot of traffic to sift through. Still, I’m looking forward to them potentially climbing up the depth chart, and I’d love to get one or both of them pulled off to the side to see how their rookie journey is coming along. Which Lions players would you like to hear more about from training camp? Share your answers in the comment section below.

Clowney, after being traded to the Seahawks in 2019, has been something akin to a ronin defensive end, making stops with several […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 23: Jadeveon Clowney #42 of the Dallas Cowboys looks on prior to the game against the Philadelphia Eagles at AT&T Stadium on November 23, 2025 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s funny how things work sometimes, isn’t it? The Houston Texans are bringing back a blast from the past, signing defensive end Jadeveon Clowney to a deal to join an already stacked defense. Back to where it began for Jadeveon Clowney: The former No. 1 overall pick of the #Texans has agreed to terms with Houston, sources tell me and @RapSheet . After an 8.5-sack season with the #Cowboys , Clowney stays in Texas in a deal done by @NFLagentandy of @UpperEdgeSports . pic.twitter.com/B8ABbDaDTF — Mike Garafolo (@MikeGarafolo) August 2, 2026 Clowney, after being traded to the Seahawks in 2019, has been something akin to a ronin defensive end, making stops with several teams on short-term deals; moving from the Seahawks to the BESFs, the Browns, the Ravens, the Panthers, and, most recently, the Cowboys. As a Cowboy, Clowney registered 8.5 sacks over 13 games, one shy of his career high. The coaching staff for the Cowboys also had nothing but positive things to say about his time with the Cowboys. Clowney’s addition to a line that already boasts Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter is going to make the Texans defense that much stronger; a defense that was already a nightmare for other teams to handle just got so much more dangerous. Welcome home, Clowney.

title: Chiefs News: Padded training camp practices begin today
summary: The latest After four full-team practices for the Kansas City Chiefs to begin training camp last week, it is now time for iron to sharpen iron. The full pads will be on Chiefs players at camp starting Monday, and it will be the start of another ramp-up period to the full-length practices we’re accustomed to […]
full_text: Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid, left, speaks with wide receiver Xavier Worthy (1) during practice at training camp on Friday, July 31, 2026, in St. Joseph. (Emily Curiel/Kansas City Star/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) The latest After four full-team practices for the Kansas City Chiefs to begin training camp last week, it is now time for iron to sharpen iron. The full pads will be on Chiefs players at camp starting Monday, and it will be the start of another ramp-up period to the full-length practices we’re accustomed to in St. Joe, according to head coach Andy Reid during a press conference last week. “We kick back just a notch, a couple of minutes there.” Five Observations from Saturday’s Practice | Chiefs Training Camp 8/1 | Chiefs.com 4. The “ramp up” to padded practices is now complete. The league-mandated process of “easing” into padded practices is now complete following Saturday’s session, setting the stage for the first padded practice of training camp on Monday morning. It’s obviously a major benchmark in the Chiefs’ preparation for the upcoming season, and keep in mind – due to league rules – Monday will mark the first time that Kansas City takes the field in pads since last season ended. The entirety of the offseason training program was limited to non-padded practices, meaning the true evaluation of certain position groups – notably the linemen on both sides of the ball – can really begin on Monday. Chiefs’ Dave Toub explains Cyrus Allen’s special-teams role after lower-leg injury | The Kansas City Star “Any time you have a rookie — everybody’s on special teams until they aren’t,” Toub said. “Until they establish themselves as a starter on offense or defense, and then we have to kind of pull back and maybe take them off of two or three phases. But initially, everybody starts off as a four-phase guy, and that’s just the way we do it. It’s worked over the years, and it’s hard to keep a guy off just because he was drafted high and all of a sudden try to pull him back and make him a special teams player later. So you start off that way, and then you wean him off the special teams as you go.” Kansas City Chiefs’ latest roster move gives a UDFA longshot a second chance to live out his NFL dream | A to Z Sports Hurkett originally joined the team as one of 20 undrafted free agents to sign following the 2026 NFL Draft. Hurkett was released following the team’s rookie minicamp. However, with a season-ending ACL injury for DE/LB Ethan Downs and a hamstring injury for DE Ashton Gillotte, Hurkett now gets another shot. The 24-year-old Hurkett is listed at 6-foot-3 and 259 pounds, boasting inside/outside flexibility from the edge rusher position. He recorded 92 total tackles, 23 tackles for loss, 14.5 sacks, and four forced fumbles over the past two seasons with the Iowa Hawkeyes. Kansas City Chiefs 2026 Season Preview: Odds, Roster, and Predictions | RG Final outlook Everything for Kansas City in 2026 flows through Mahomes’ recovery. The early signs from camp, an accelerated rehab timeline and full participation in team drills, are encouraging, and the addition of Kenneth Walker III gives the offense a more balanced identity than it’s had in years. The defense is betting heavily on youth around Chris Jones, with Delane and Woods needing to develop quickly. If Mahomes is truly ready for Week 1 and the young defenders take the expected step forward, Kansas City has the pieces to erase last year’s disappointment and get back into the AFC’s championship picture. Nick Bolton Says Chiefs Will ‘Never’ Replace Leo Chenal, but Here’s Who’s Trying to Do It | Sports Illustrated “You’re never going to replace that guy with just one person,” Bolton said. “The energy he has on the team and in the building, also on the football field. You see his effort on field goal blocks and defensive plays. He goes and plays three-tech for us sometimes, he blitzes, plays a little bit of coverage, a little bit of everything — special teams as well. It’s going to be all hands on deck. I think they’re trying to find guys that can mimic the things he does well, but obviously he was a great player for us.” Around the NFL Pass rusher Jadeveon Clowney reaches deal to reunite with Texans | ESPN Clowney confirmed a report by NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport and Mike Garafolo that he had agreed to a contract with the Texans, telling the Houston Chronicle that he has “grown up and learned the game a lot more since” last playing with Houston in 2018. “I feel like I can help the younger guys. I’ve learned how to lead and what it takes to get to a Super Bowl. I feel like I can help this team,” he told the newspaper. Saints place 2024 second-round WR Ja’Lynn Polk on Reserve/Retired list | NFL.com He then suffered a season-ending shoulder injury during New England’s training camp in August 2025. A few weeks later, the Patriots traded Polk and a 2028 seventh-round pick to the Saints in exchange for a 2027 sixth-round selection. The goal was to rehab and bounce back in Year 3 in a fresh environment. Instead, Polk has made the decision to hang it up. After taking coaching job at Georgia Tech, DeAndre Hopkins says he isn’t retired | Pro Football Talk “I haven’t retired from the NFL,” Hopkins posted Saturday on Twitter, via Andy Backstrom of Yahoo Sports. “But if you’re a WR and you want to be great, come to Georgia Tech football.” Hopkins, 34, is keeping himself busy as he waits for another opportunity. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Chiefs training camp: All eyes are on Xavier Worthy’s durability On Saturday, Worthy had a strong practice, catching at least two tough, downfield passes from Mahomes. After the second, Worthy reportedly left the field with a designation for his shoulder, but all signs point to the rest being closer to precautionary than worrisome. But it’s not just Go and Post routes Worthy is working on refining; it’s his entire route tree. He explained to the media that due to his hurt shoulder, he was limited in the way he could play last season. “Last year was kind of hard to look at [because] my routes kind of got changed,” Worthy told reporters. “I couldn’t run a lot of the things that I would normally run and couldn’t run it in the way that I would want to.” From The Feed Follow Arrowhead Pride on Social Media Facebook: Like our page Instagram: @ArrowheadPride X: Follow @ArrowheadPride AP Staff on X: See complete list 90.9 The Bridge on X: Follow @909thebridge

title: 10 Biggest Chiefs Questions: What is team’s identity for this season?
summary: Arguably the most important thing a good football team has is an identity. An identity is a play style that separates you from the rest of the league. It’s what you do best and what you lean on to win big games. The cool thing about football is there are many different shapes that can […]
full_text: Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid observes players during practice at training camp on Friday, July 31, 2026, in St. Joseph. (Emily Curiel/Kansas City Star/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) Arguably the most important thing a good football team has is an identity. An identity is a play style that separates you from the rest of the league. It’s what you do best and what you lean on to win big games. The cool thing about football is there are many different shapes that can form an identity. For example, the Peyton Manning era with the Indianapolis Colts was defined by their elite passing game, with Manning and multiple Hall of Fame receivers in Reggie Wayne and Marvin Harrison. The Pittsburgh Steelers and Baltimore Ravens have long held an identity of a tough, physical defense built on front seven play. The Seattle Seahawks built two Super Bowl teams within 15 years based on dominant defenses. It’s cool to see the shift and change in identity over time among the great teams. The New England Patriots under Bill Belichick and Tom Brady were a prime example of this. When the franchise first started winning Super Bowls, it was because of a dominant defense. In the early 2010s, the organization acquired players like wide receivers Wes Welker, Randy Moss, and tight ends Rob Gronkowski and Aaron Hernandez in a shift to having an all-time offense. The Kansas City Chiefs have undergone a similar arc to the Patriots in modern history. From 2018-2022, the Chiefs’ identity was built on having a dominant, explosive offense. Quarterback Patrick Mahomes was a player the league had never seen with his combination of arm talent, athleticism, and feel for the game. Wide receiver Tyreek Hill was potentially the fastest player ever who grew into being an elite receiver. Tight end Travis Kelce was arguably the best pass-catching tight end in football history. The offense was built around those three players and had strong supporting pieces around them. Offensive tackles Eric Fisher and Mitchell Schwartz were great bookends to keeping Mahomes upright. Wide receiver Sammy Watkins wasn’t always healthy and consistent, but his best moments in the playoffs proved to be huge. But, like the Patriots, the Chiefs had to shift the identity to the other side of the ball to continue winning championships after the 2022 season. Kelce started to decline in 2023, which took the offense from the best in the league to closer to league average. The wide receiver play fell off a cliff, the running game was nonexistent, and the tackle play was always shaky. Fortunately, the Chiefs had spent years building up their defense to the point where it was dominant in 2023. Defensive tackle Chris Jones has been a stalwart throughout this entire dynasty, but the team had finally surrounded him with elite personnel. Cornerbacks Trent McDuffie and L’Jarius Sneed dominated the entire 2023 season by blanketing every receiver in man coverage. Over the past two seasons, something has changed. The Chiefs have lacked an identity, something the team differentiates itself from other contenders with. This wasn’t an issue for most of the 2024 season. The team went 15-1 in the games that Mahomes started. However, there was always something off about that team, never really playing dominant football. The team did a great job closing out games, but each one was a slog. The team was good enough on both sides of the ball, and didn’t have a calling card. That lack of an elite characteristic caught up to them in Super Bowl LIX against the Philadelphia Eagles . The Eagles, with an elite defense, stomped the Chiefs’ offense, which had less talent and simply wasn’t elite. The Chiefs did stop the run that game, but struggled to cover the downfield passes the coverage would’ve more likely stopped in 2023. The Eagles had a clear identity to win and destroyed a Chiefs team that never found theirs. This lack of identity became an even bigger problem in 2025. The close-game results flipped in the opposite direction. Some of that is bad luck, but the team still had similar core issues: it wasn’t elite on either side of the ball and couldn’t lean on anything. The struggles at receiver and in the run game capped the offense’s ceiling. The defense had bled talent and couldn’t get pressure. Moving it forward to 2026, I’m not sure what the identity of this team is going to be. The front office didn’t go all-out on addressing one side of the ball as has been done previously. Instead, they made moves on both sides of the ball to address weaknesses. With running back Kenneth Walker in Kansas City, will we finally see the Chiefs build the offensive identity around a strong run game? Is that enough for them to have an elite offense? This team still has receiver problems and tackle concerns, so I don’t think they can build an identity around an elite passing game. They do have an elite offensive line in the run game, so maybe having a dynamic running back can let them build a team around that. Defensively, it’s hard to know what it will be because they have so many young players. I’m not sure what the scheme or playstyle will look like yet. The question is whether those young players can get up to speed quick enough for them to have a defensive identity. Regardless, for the Chiefs to return to being an elite team, they have to find a calling card they’re elite at. Even if it’s not this season, they need to find something to build around long-term in hopes of returning to the top of the NFL.
author: Nate Christensen

title: Chiefs training camp: All eyes are on Xavier Worthy’s durability
summary: Friends, we did it; we made it through the long, and at times, seemingly endless road that is the offseason. And I’ll be honest, there were times I didn’t think I would make it—let’s face it, a life without Kansas City Chiefs football is more boring than the drive from Kansas City to the Colorado […]
full_text: ST. JOSEPH, MO - JULY 29: Xavier Worthy #1 walks to the field before practice during the Kansas City Chiefs training camp on July 29, 2026 at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Friends, we did it; we made it through the long, and at times, seemingly endless road that is the offseason. And I’ll be honest, there were times I didn’t think I would make it—let’s face it, a life without Kansas City Chiefs football is more boring than the drive from Kansas City to the Colorado border. But as you can see from the footage captured by the captain of our ship here at Arrowhead Pride , Ron Kopp Jr., we are back, baby! Mahomes trying to push the ball downfield in 7on7s today. Tries for X against Nohl Williams deep here pic.twitter.com/9OkrGg1UmA — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) July 30, 2026 In the video, you can see quarterback Patrick Mahomes try to connect with wide receiver Xavier Worthy on a deep ball down the sideline, with cornerback Nohl Williams in coverage. Although Worthy has a step on Williams, the ball carries Worthy out of the end zone, and he’s only able to get one foot down. That has been a theme early in his career, but with a new wide receivers coach in Chad O’Shea and a disappointing sophomore season marred by a shoulder injury , Chiefs fans are excited to see him healthy and opening it up down the field. It’s something the team wasn’t able to work on until camp. Worthy donned a yellow non-contact jersey during OTAs earlier this summer, as he worked his way back from surgery to repair his injured shoulder this offseason. Speaking to the media on Friday afternoon, Worthy spoke about his road back from his injury. “Last year I was never 100%,” explained Worthy. “I was never going to be 100% until I got the surgery. So I got the surgery, been working on it, building muscle mass, obviously working at it in the offseason, getting stronger and obviously building that shoulder back.” As for working on the deep ball with Mahomes, Worthy said that with the Chiefs star quarterback battling his own injury, it’s something they are going to continue to work on to develop their chemistry. “Whenever we got the opportunity, you know, he was limited in OTAs. So, we tried our hardest to work at it, and we’re going to continue working on it throughout this camp.” Xavier Worthy cont – If this was the play (seems like it based on reports), he does land onto his Right shoulder (surgical side) but good to see no bracing or guarding after standing up. Fits several comments that he seemed fine as he left practice pic.twitter.com/ztB1fD2o8t — Jeff Mueller, PT, DPT (@jmthrivept) August 1, 2026 On Saturday, Worthy had a strong practice, catching at least two tough, downfield passes from Mahomes. After the second, Worthy reportedly left the field with a designation for his shoulder, but all signs point to the rest being closer to precautionary than worrisome. But it’s not just Go and Post routes Worthy is working on refining; it’s his entire route tree. He explained to the media that due to his hurt shoulder, he was limited in the way he could play last season. “Last year was kind of hard to look at [because] my routes kind of got changed,” Worthy told reporters. “I couldn’t run a lot of the things that I would normally run and couldn’t run it in the way that I would want to.” Still, there are things that he could have done better, and that’s what he worked on this summer. “I was kind of just looking at it as in what would I do in this situation when I was watching the film,” Worthy said. “It was a lot of things that I could have done and could have done better, and obviously I worked at it [in the] offseason.” Worthy looks to play a pivotal role in the Chiefs’ passing game this season, but with a pre-draft frame of just 5 feet 11 inches tall and 165 pounds, durability will be a question mark that Worthy will have to continually answer until he shows he can make it through an entire 17-game season and hopefully a playoff run without suffering an injury that sidelines or limits him for multiple games. It will be crucial that he can: Mahomes needs all the weapons he can get if Kansas City is to right the wrong that was their 6-11 season last year.

title: Veteran OL linked to Chargers in training camp free agency
summary: The Los Angeles Chargers are hoping for their offensive line to improve going into the 2026 season. Having Rashaun Slater and Joe Alt return from injury to book in the offensive line will be crucial, but they also need some upgrades on the interior. NFL.com contributor Grant Gordon believes the team could sign former first-round […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - JANUARY 04: Kevin Zeitler #70 of the Tennessee Titans looks on prior to a game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at EverBank Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Rich Storry/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Los Angeles Chargers are hoping for their offensive line to improve going into the 2026 season. Having Rashaun Slater and Joe Alt return from injury to book in the offensive line will be crucial, but they also need some upgrades on the interior. NFL.com contributor Grant Gordon believes the team could sign former first-round pick Kevin Zeitler in free agency. “L.A. will have new starters at guard — either rookie Jake Slaughter, converting from center, free-agent signees Cole Strange or Kayode Awosika, or the roller coaster that is Trevor Penning. After overwhelming injury woes along the O-line a season ago, the Bolts know the importance of depth, and Zeitler could be a starting upgrade. Fourteen seasons in, Zeitler is a plus-option mercenary who’s started double-digit games every year he’s played and was a Pro Bowler for the Ravens just three years ago. The Chargers like ex-Ravens players and former first-rounders on the line,” Gordon wrote. Zeitler, 36, spent his first five years with the Cincinnati Bengals after being selected with the 27th overall pick in the 2012 NFL draft. He bounced around after that, playing with the Cleveland Browns, New York Giants, Baltimore Ravens, Detroit Lions and last season with the Tennessee Titans. Zeitler’s experience could give the Chargers some insurance on the offensive line in case one of their players gets injured or doesn’t pan out as well as they had hoped. BFTB community, how do you feel about Zeitler’s fit with the Chargers? Let us know in the comments section below.

author: JB Scott

title: Predicting the Rams’ award winners for 2026
summary: Every NFL season produces its own collection of unforgettable performances. Some players meet lofty expectations, while others emerge from relative obscurity to become key contributors. By the time the regular season concludes, every successful team can point to a handful of players whose performances shaped the year. The Los Angeles Rams will likely be no […]
full_text: Every NFL season produces its own collection of unforgettable performances. Some players meet lofty expectations, while others emerge from relative obscurity to become key contributors. By the time the regular season concludes, every successful team can point to a handful of players whose performances shaped the year. The Los Angeles Rams will likely be no different in 2026. With established veterans, ascending young talent, and an intriguing rookie class all competing for playing time, there are plenty of candidates to leave a lasting mark on the season. Rather than waiting until January to hand out team honors, let’s make some predictions before the season gets underway. Which players will define the Rams’ campaign? Here are six team awards to consider heading into 2026. Team MVP No award carries more weight than Team MVP. This honor belongs to the player whose impact extends beyond the stat sheet and consistently gives the Rams their best chance to win each week. Whether it’s a franchise quarterback, a dominant defensive star, or an offensive playmaker who takes over games, the Team MVP often becomes the face of the season. Leadership, consistency, durability, and clutch performances all factor into this selection. Prediction: Matthew Stafford Stafford will lead the Rams to a 14-3 record and first round bye. He hits the 40 touchdown threshold again but doesn’t quite get to the 46 mark that he had last year. Offensive Player of the Year The Rams have assembled plenty of offensive talent capable of producing a standout season. This award recognizes the player who drives the offense through explosive plays, consistency, and game-changing production. It doesn’t necessarily have to go to the team’s MVP. Sometimes another offensive player elevates the entire unit through big plays, reliability, or a breakout campaign that exceeds expectations. Prediction: Puka Nacua Nacua is Stafford’s right hand man. Nacua will continue to receive a large volume of targets, especially in 3rd down situations when the chains need to be moved. There’s a strong chance that Nacua puts up his best season to date in a contract year. Defensive Player of the Year Championship-caliber teams are built on defense just as much as offense. The Rams have invested heavily in building an aggressive, athletic defensive unit, and someone will likely emerge as the centerpiece. Whether it’s through sacks, turnovers, tackles for loss, or simply making offenses game plan around them every week, this award honors the defender who has the biggest impact on winning football games. Prediction: Myles Garrett An Aaron Donald return could make this a split vote but Garrett will likely have the most on his resume by the end of the season. Garrett will push to break his own record of 23.5 sacks. Rookie of the Year Every draft class brings excitement and opportunity. Some rookies contribute immediately, while others steadily carve out larger roles as the season progresses. This award isn’t always about posting the biggest statistics. Sometimes it’s about exceeding expectations, earning meaningful snaps, or becoming an important contributor sooner than anticipated. Prediction: CJ Daniels The only two considerations for Rookie of the Year will be CJ Daniels and Max Klare. Daniels will find himself on the field from the halfway point of the season and will find the endzone a total of three times. Most Improved Player Development has long been one of the Rams’ organizational strengths. Every season, one or two players take a significant leap after gaining experience, improving their technique, or earning a larger opportunity. The Most Improved Player award recognizes the individual who makes the biggest jump from last season to this one. Whether it’s a young starter, former reserve, or someone returning from adversity, improvement often becomes one of the biggest stories of the year. Prediction: Terrance Ferguson Ferguson delivers in year two as a starting tight end alongside of Colby Parkinson. Unsung Hero Not every valuable player receives national recognition. Every successful roster features dependable contributors who consistently make winning plays without dominating headlines. The Unsung Hero may not lead the team in statistics or receive Pro Bowl consideration, but teammates and coaches understand just how valuable that player is. It could be a special teams standout, a versatile role player, an offensive lineman, or a defender whose impact goes far beyond the box score. Prediction: Warren McClendon The offensive line will need to remain healthy for the Rams season to be effective. McClendon locks down the right tackle spot in the wake of Rob Havenstein’s offseason retirement. McClendon’s steady presence on the right side paves the way for another big year from Stafford.
author: Steven Ridings

title: How many Rams are in the elite tier at their respective positions?
summary: Stop us if you’ve heard this before: The Los Angeles Rams have the best roster in the NFL. That’s not news to anyone who’s been paying attention this offseason, and while it doesn’t guarantee a championship by any means it does illustrate why so many outlets (and sportsbooks) are favoring the Rams to win the […]
full_text: Stop us if you’ve heard this before: The Los Angeles Rams have the best roster in the NFL. That’s not news to anyone who’s been paying attention this offseason, and while it doesn’t guarantee a championship by any means it does illustrate why so many outlets (and sportsbooks) are favoring the Rams to win the Super Bowl this year. Today, we’re taking a different sort of look at why the Rams have such a strong roster: How many players on this team are in the truly elite tier of their respective positions? There is a ton of depth both offensively and defensively for this team, but where are the no-doubt best-of-the-best players? Let’s dive into each position group and identify which Rams are clearly at the top of the class: Quarterback There’s a generally accepted upper echelon at quarterback, usually including Patrick Mahomes, Josh Allen and Lamar Jackson, but it’s nearly impossible to go any farther without including Matthew Stafford at this point. And if you want to put him in front of any of those aforementioned three, you won’t meet much pushback these days after Stafford just won the league MVP award . Who else could you put ahead of Stafford in the elite tier right now? Joe Burrow? No. Justin Herbert? No. Drake Maye? He was great in his runner-up campaign last year but it’s too early to go that far. It depends on how you want to define “elite” in this case, but Stafford is no worse than being right on the cusp if not all the way in the thick of that tier. Running back The Rams have two good to very good running backs on the roster, both of whom both put up solid counting stats and impressive advanced numbers. But no one is going to confuse either Kyren Williams or Blake Corum with the short list of the best backs in the league right this second. Wide receiver At this point, Puka Nacua is easily on the Mount Rushmore of wide receivers in the league right now. It’s Nacua, Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Ja’Marr Chase and Justin Jefferson at the top of the position, then a mass quantity of players battling for fifth-best and beyond. Pro Football Focus ranked Nacua as the best wide receiver in the league for 2026, and in 2025 he finished third in Offensive Player of the Year voting. His combination of unique skill set and production easily establishes his place among the NFL’s best receivers. Tight end There are plenty of good and interesting tight ends on this roster, but none crack the very upper echelon at this position relative to their peers. Colby Parkinson unlocks a ton for the Rams’ offense and Terrance Ferguson has a massive upside, but those guys aren’t quite on the level of a George Kittle (pending health), Trey McBride or Brock Bowers. Offensive line Tackles are in a strong place league-wide right now, to the point that the executives polled for ESPN’s position-by-position top-10 rankings didn’t offer up a single vote for Alaric Jackson. He’s a well-above average tackle, but it’s not an easy group to break into at the top. Along the interior, there’s plenty of quality talent but again, it’s hard to usher any of that group, from Steve Avila to Kevn Dotson to Coleman Shelton, into truly rarified air as things stand today. Defensive line Kobie Turner deserves plenty of hype, attention and adulation, but he probably still falls just outside the top tier on the defensive line. There’s just so much talent in the league right now. Jeffery Simmons, Leonard Williams, Jalen Carter, there are so many high-quality interior players right now. If you want to break it down to an extremely granular level, though, there’s a legitimate argument for putting Poona Ford at the very top of a run-stopping specialist ranking. Edge rusher The Rams have the best edge rusher in the NFL. Myles Garrett might be the best defensive player in the NFL, period. This one is obvious. Linebacker It’s almost become a meme when you listen to national analysis of the Rams that the franchise just won’t spend major resources on linebacker. Which, in the long run, is fine, considering how good the front, the edge and the secondary are. Nate Landman and Omar Speights are serviceable, which is good enough for this team, it’s just not going to land them near anyone’s top linebacker rankings. Safety This is another reliable, good position group for the Rams but one that lacks a true superstar. Both Kams, Curl and Kinchens, are valuable pieces to this defense and would play a big role for pretty much any team. They’re not Kyle Hamilton or Derwin James, though. Cornerback After being the biggest weakness on the defense a year ago, the Rams have not only turned it into a legitimate strength in one offseason, but they’ve added a bona fide elite talent in the room, too. Trent McDuffie is that guy. He’s arguably the best slot corner in the NFL right now, and even on the boundary he’s far above average. With that kind of versatility and a floor of “really good” compared to a ceiling of “best in the business,” it’s an easy call with McDuffie.
author: Brendan Dzwierzynski

title: Rams safeties plan to “nickel and dime” the opposition
summary: To a man, the Los Angeles Rams safety unit are all on board for 2026. More importantly, the room appears set for future years. New money was doled to primary starters Quentin Lake and Kamren Curl, locking them through 2028. Kamren Kinchens is still on his rookie deal and the rest of the individuals in […]
full_text: To a man, the Los Angeles Rams safety unit are all on board for 2026. More importantly, the room appears set for future years. New money was doled to primary starters Quentin Lake and Kamren Curl, locking them through 2028. Kamren Kinchens is still on his rookie deal and the rest of the individuals in the unit do not have enough accrued seasons to leave on their own, L.A. has them tied up if they so choose. 2026 should be an exciting year for the Rams secondary. Alongside the shiny new cornerback additions, reports out of camp are that the L.A. defensive braintrust is really sold on the safety group’s veteran leadership, versatility, and communication. And much should be expected from the safety unit, last year the Rams leaned heavily onto dime (six secondary players) formations, their 32.4 percent usage rate (per Next Gen Stats ). That really stands out when compared to other NFL teams, most use it under 10 percent. The Rams also used “big” nickel, inserting a safety as the fifth secondary player, on 30.3 percent of defensive snaps. Guess who the ILBers are? You're right if you said Jaylen McCollough and Cobie Durant It's a dime — but it aligned like a base defense Rams have 2 DL, 3 OLBer — this is basically base defense with 2 DBs playing LBer looks just like a 3-4 with gold front #Rams #RamsHouse pic.twitter.com/csluv5j1ao — Jim Youngblood 53 (@53_jim70721) October 20, 2024 With the depth at safety, it will be tough to move up the food chain for the players towards the bottom. Let’s look at them all. A pair to draw to Quentin Lake – 6’1” 205 lb. Lake has started 30 of his 50 pro games and although he missed seven games last season with an elbow injury, the Rams re-upped him last season with a three-year extension for a little over $38mil. He was on track for his best pro season in 2025 before injury struck. Pro Football Focus gave him scores of 75.1 overall (13th) broken into 72.9 for coverage (19th) and 74.6 against the run (29th). Defensive coordinator Chris Shula calls him a “coach on the field” and the “glue” of the defense. L.A. moves him around the defensive formation and recently have used in the “STAR” role, as a safety/slot/linebacker hybrid. Not a thumper, but good wrap-up tackler. Strong in zone coverage, using his vision, understanding of routes, read/react ability. Average athleticism, but loose-limbed and has good play speed. Kamren Curl – 6’1” 207 lb. Solid but not spectacular safety. Consistently produced over six years in the league. Curl has proven durable and sports a well-rounded game. Best suited working underneath. Last year over 10000+ snaps, he accrued a 77.8 (9th) Pro Football Focus overall grade, punctuated with a 87.9 score (2nd) against the run and 71.9 (15th) versus the pass. The Rams rewarded him with a three-year $36-39mil extension this past March. At 27, Curl should be entering his prime. He’s improved on his missed tackles and coverage over his NFL tenure. Excellent versatility and now has a deep understanding of what the Rams defense is supposed to be doing. Sure tackler, not a banger, but physical when fitting gaps at the line of scrimmage. Takes good angles and and flows to the ball fluidly. Above average speed/athleticism with good arm length. Best in zone coverage, tacks ball well and although he allows a fairly high completion rate, he’s quite stingy giving up yards after catch. The future? Kamren Kinchens – 5’11” 203 lb. Comfortably settled in as the Rams S#3 and arguably has the most playmaker potential in the Rams safety room. Because the Rams use so many multi-safety personnel groupings (big nickel or dime), Kinchens gets a fair share of defensive snaps, 1356 over his first two seasons. L.A. has used him predominantly deep. Although he didn’t test well at the NFL Combine or Pro Day, Kinchens came into the league with reputation as a ball hawk. In his first two pro seasons, Kinchens has given glimpses of his ability to track the ball with six interceptions, 12 passes broken up, and three fumbles recovered. He makes up for average athleticism with loose hips and good footwork. Stellar vision, instincts, and understanding space get him a jump on the football. Willing in run support, comes downhill very well and plays with an aggressive style. Angles still need some work, but he’s improved on wrapping up tackles instead of always going for the big hit. Jaylen McCollough – 6’ 211 lb. Started 51 out of 60 SEC games at Tennessee, but still went undrafted. He impressed right away with the Rams and made the roster as a rookie. Played in every game and tied for the team lead in interceptions with four. In Year 2, he did not match the picked off passes, but made strides with the rest of his game. Again, he played in every game, also adding six starts and upped his production number across the board. High-effort player with physical play style. Early on, he was best suited underneath and the Rams often used him as a pseudo-linebacker. As 2025 progressed he saw a fair share of action deeper in the secondary. Not a gifted athlete, bit of a stocky build. Plays faster and looks more athletic than his pedestrian Pro Day testing. Wins with good instincts assignment-based play. Also an important piece on special teams. Roster battle Nick Anderson – 5’11” 195 lb. Safety that plays with a linebacker’s attitude. Very versatile, ability to play that role as an overhang, as a traditional underneath strong safety, or deep, in Cover2 and possibly single high. I say possibly, because although his instincts, read react skills, and ball tracking fit, it remains to be answered how his long speed will translate deep in the NFL. Doesn’t have elite twitch, but strong football IQ and play recognition help him to quick-trigger and play fast. While likely best suited for zone coverage, Anderson does have enough move skills and the requisite physicality to match tight ends 1on1. He times hits well in the secondary and is very physical at the catch point. Strong ball tracking and hawking. Good hands, eyes and the body control to snag awry passes. Stellar in run support. Solid tackler, generally breaks down and wraps up. Anticipates well and takes good angles in pursuit. Tanner Ingle – 5’9” 179 lb. Enters his fourth season in L.A. Ingle was active in three regular-season games and one in the playoffs last year, his only action with the Rams, logging three defensive snaps and 43 on special teams. He’s an aggressive, overachieving safety who is under-sized and lacks elite athleticism. Ferocious downhill defender whose best work is done around the line of scrimmage. There’s no doubt that he’s a downhill missile in run support and on short passes, but he needs a lot of coverage work. To the point of being too small for an NFL safety and currently lacks coverage skills to work out of the slot. Can his toughness overcome his size around the line of scrimmage? Fits the Rams mold of hot motor and football instincts. HIs ball pursuit and willingness to bang heads makes him fit and is his path to a possible role HIs relentless, pursuit, effort, and willingness to bang heads makes him fit for a possible role as special teams demon. Nate Valcarcel – 6’ 194 lb. Recruited as a cornerback in college, Valcarcel switched to safety midway through his tenure. Lean build. Valcarcel’s pursuit to the ball, both on the ground and through the air stands out. Played a lot of single-high safety. Versus the run, he shows good pursuit angles, quick read/react processing, and an aggressive demeanor. His tackling is good, breaking down and getting himself under control, and wrapping up. Against the pass, his cornerback past clearly shows. He reads the quarterback well, shows route recognition, and is adept at both breaking downhill or flipping his hips open and turning to cover deep routes. Valcarcel is an anomaly in his second training camp with the Rams, he appears to have the game and traits of a true free safety. Can he adapt his range, ball-hawking, and pursuit…
author: Venie Randy Soares

title: C.J. Daniels not only receiver surprising at Rams camp
summary: Mario Williams knows what it’s like to be at the bottom and work his way up to a job, and based on camp reports he could make it difficult for the L.A. Rams coaching staff when it’s time to chose the last receiver on the roster. The second-year undrafted free agent could make a push […]
full_text: LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - JULY 29: Mario Williams #14 of the Los Angeles Rams runs after the catch during training camp at Loyola Marymount University on July 29, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images Mario Williams knows what it’s like to be at the bottom and work his way up to a job, and based on camp reports he could make it difficult for the L.A. Rams coaching staff when it’s time to chose the last receiver on the roster. The second-year undrafted free agent could make a push against the likes of Xavier Smith and Konata Mumpfield if he continues to stack days like the last one. In camp observation from Saturday’s practice, team writers Stu Jackson and Zach Edwards highlighted Edwards as a surprising standout : Wide receiver Mario Williams makes some noise: After a quiet camp so far, Williams made a statement on Day 6. He had multiple receptions over the field, including a diving catch on a scramble drill from Bennett that brought applause from the crowd at LMU. Will Williams be this year’s most unexpected player on the Rams’ 53-man roster? Who is Mario Williams anyway? A four-star prospect in the 2021 recruiting class , Williams chose to attend Oklahoma when he was the 15th-ranked receiver in the country. For context, that’s the same high school graduating class as Brian Thomas, Emeka Egbuka, Marvin Harrison, Malik Nabers, Xavier Worthy, and Keion Coleman. Williams was ranked higher by 247 Sports than Harrison and Nabers. After catching 35 passes for 381 yards when he was paired with Caleb Williams, Mario also followed head coach Lincoln Riley to USC in 2022 with the quarterback. That first season for the Trojans was rather successful, including 40 catches for 631 yards and five touchdowns, helping Caleb Williams win the Heisman. However, almost nothing went right for 8-5 USC in 2023. Almost everybody’s production went down, including Mario Williams, finishing with just 29 catches for 305 yards and two touchdowns. With Caleb going to the NFL, and receivers like Makai Lemon and Zachariah Branch set to be the future at USC, Mario transferred again. But this time, he was going to Tulane, and he would have to reclaim his status as a highly-touted receiver prospect once again. Williams 2025 season Tulane doesn’t have the same reputation or competition as USC or Oklahoma, but they could give Mario Williams a chance to be a WR1. SI’s Tulane blog highlighted some of his best traits : Mario Williams immediately brings explosiveness to Tulane’s offense. On any given play, Williams can take a bubble screen to the house and is one of the most difficult players to catch in open space in college football. Williams did not make it to USC because of his inability to catch the ball consistently. It is common for some of the most explosive receivers to struggle with this trait because they are such threats after the catch that they focus on their next move before securing the football. That is the case with Mario Williams. So, what does that mean for his role in the offense next season? Honestly, it does not mean much. Williams is so talented that keeping him off the field is impossible. In addition to his explosiveness, he brings an unmatched, infectious level of energy to the offense. Some receivers, like Odell Beckham Jr., are so productive that teams are willing to live with the drops. That is the case with Mario Williams. A year before Jon Sumrall helped the program reach the College Football Playoffs, the head coach focused his passing offense on Williams: 60 catches for 1,031 yards, 6 touchdowns. That type of production didn’t help Williams get drafted, but it did rebuild him from an afterthought at USC to a player now going into his second year of Rams training camp. Mario Williams on Rams Without an invite to the combine, Williams was left to workout at the Tulane pro day, where speed was not his strong suit. He was only around a 4.50 despite being 5’9, 178. Sumrall, who is now the head coach at Florida, explained it’s never been about speed with Mario : “Mario’s best trait is not speed, it’s not ball skills, it’s competitive nature. We would do our winter workouts last January and February and he had no problem on who he was matched up with that morning of the workout because we would pair guys up one on one all day. He would walk into the workout and let the guy know, you’re going to lose today because you’re matched up with me. I’m going to win.” It’s that competitive nature that could catch the attention of Sean McVay. The Rams only have two receivers who are 100-percent, undeniably locked onto the roster, Puka Nacua and Davante Adams. And they were even open to trading one of those players earlier this year if it meant getting A.J. Brown. Of course, C.J. Daniels and Jordan Whittington might be 90 or 95 or even 98-percent likely to make the roster. I’m just saying, only two are 100-percent and that’s because L.A. didn’t make any major moves for a receiver like they could have if they had drafted Lemon or anybody higher than the fifth round. But if we assume that Nacua, Adams, Daniels, and Whittington are on the roster, that leaves at least one open spot. Maybe two. Potentially three. Mumpfield and Smith are the two next in line. Then there’s Tyler Scott, Brennan Presley, Tru Edwards, and Williams. Saturday was just one day of practice and the next standout could be Scott, Presley, or Edwards. When it comes time for preseason action, these are also the receivers most likely to be out there playing. If Mario Williams (46 yards, 1 TD in 2025 preseason ) has 100 yards in that first preseason game, maybe the Rams don’t use him the next time. Just as it could be true for anybody else who has a debut like that this year. Stetson Bennett IV (4) to Mario Williams (1)* Los Angeles Rams 38 yards pic.twitter.com/tT4GKuKqRA — NFL Touchdown Videos (@NFLTDsVideos) August 17, 2025 It was only two years ago that Williams was being pushed out of a job at USC, where he had followed his coach and quarterback, needing a new opportunity to prove himself. He did it then. With more practices like the last one, could he do it again?

title: The mystery of the Rams’ punt return role
summary: It was peculiar when the Los Angeles Rams stood pat and did not acquire a return specialist over the offseason. The memory of Xavier Smith muffing a punt deep in LA territory to effective spot the Seattle Seahawks a touchdown during the NFC Championship game is unshakable. But Smith doesn’t seem to be the answer […]
full_text: Westchester, - August 01: Running back Kyren Williams #23 with head coach Sean McVay of the Los Angeles Rams during the Los Angeles Rams training camp on the campus of Loyola Marymount University in Westchester on Saturday, August 1, 2026. (Photo by Keith Birmingham/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images It was peculiar when the Los Angeles Rams stood pat and did not acquire a return specialist over the offseason. The memory of Xavier Smith muffing a punt deep in LA territory to effective spot the Seattle Seahawks a touchdown during the NFC Championship game is unshakable. But Smith doesn’t seem to be the answer for 2026 either. The Rams have seemingly lost confidence in his sure-handedness. Instead, LA seems set on deploying veteran running back Kyren Williams as the primary punt returner. That is even more peculiar than doing nothing over the offseason. There are several tangential questions that come to mind if Williams truly does hold onto this role. This is a Rams whodunnit. It’s time to put on our detective caps and get to the bottom of this mystery. Kyren Williams took the first two punt return reps at #Rams practice 👀 pic.twitter.com/PntuQDGuLW — 𝙏𝙞𝙥𝙞𝙙𝙞𝙨 🐐⛷️ (@ShoGotNow) August 1, 2026 1 – Does Smith have a place on the roster? One element working in Smith’s favor in terms of making the team is that he’s probably the fastest and most true vertical threat the Rams have at receiver. He showed flashes late last year and into the playoffs that he could potentially be a more affordable alternative to Tutu Atwell’s contributions. Filling such a role is inherently valuable in a receiving corps that generally lacks long speed. But there seems to be no possible way that Los Angeles could keep Smith if his utility on special teams comes to an end, unless he can carve out a role outside of his traditional usage as the returner. The Rams seem set with at least their top five receivers. They may also need to keep five tight ends in order to deploy their heavier personnel packages and insure against the inevitability of injury. Receivers: Puka Nacua Davante Adams Jordan Whittington CJ Daniels Konata Mumpfield Tight Ends: Terrance Ferguson Max Klare Colby Parkinson Tyler Higbee Davis Allen These two positions will trend together to play into a numbers crunch. Smith seems like the obvious and easiest first man out. 2 – What does this say about Williams? There’s no doubt that Blake Corum is an emerging player in the backfield. He rushed for over 700 yards and cut Williams workload to roughly 52% of the team’s overall carries. Could Corum unseat Williams as the top back in 2026? Crazier things have happened. Corum is the more explosive runner. What if the Rams are content trotting Williams out as the punt returner because they realize he is losing ground to Corum? It would be mildly surprising but it does make sense on the surface that they’d tried to find utility for him elsewhere. LA historically does not invest in veteran running backs following the Todd Gurley dilemma. They made an exception with Williams. On the other hand, it does seem odd that they’d use their most expensive running back as a returner. One important note to keep in mind: Williams’ contract suggests this is his last year with the team . 3 – Can returner be addressed later? It does seem plausible that the Rams could find a return man when the rest of the NFL cuts down to their 53-man rosters. It’s how they’ve found the likes of Jojo Natson and others over the years. This year could be different. Making the initial 53 in Los Angeles in 2026 is no small task. This is one of the most competitive roster battles we’ve seen in during the Sean McVay era. Would the Rams really feel comfortable moving on from a known commodity in order to bring in an outside player for a niche role? It feels unlikely right now.
