title: What Klint Kubiak must do to get most out of quarterback Kirk Cousins
summary: The last time Klint Kubiak and Kirk Cousins were together back in 2019 in Minnesota, the coach was a up-and-coming 32-year-old offensive coordinator while the quarterback had turned 31 years old and entered his eighth year in the NFL. After spending three seasons with the Vikings and making other stops along the way, the duo […]
full_text: Jun 9, 2026; Henderson, NV, USA; Las Vegas Raiders coach Klint Kubiak (left) and quarterback Kirk Cousins (8) during minicamp at Intermountain Health Performance Center. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | Kirby Lee-Imagn Images The last time Klint Kubiak and Kirk Cousins were together back in 2019 in Minnesota, the coach was a up-and-coming 32-year-old offensive coordinator while the quarterback had turned 31 years old and entered his eighth year in the NFL. After spending three seasons with the Vikings and making other stops along the way, the duo are seen as the beacons of hope for the Silver & Black heading into 2026. Kubiak, now 39, is well into his first season as an NFL head coach helming the Las Vegas Raiders. And one of the biggest pieces of his upcoming offense is Cousins, a soon-to-be 38-year-old veteran (on August 19) that’s been identified as the team’s starting quarterback while prized No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft Fernando Mendoza is in watch, learn, and develop mode. “I think in this league, it’s kind of one day at a time,” Cousins said when asked what it means to be named the definitive starter after the Raiders training camp session this past Wednesday. “You’re only as good as your last throw, your last practice. You try to every day go out and earn that opportunity and never take anything for granted.” The reunions extends beyond the head coach and quarterback. There’s Andrew Janocko, who is one of Kubiak’s most trusted lieutenants as current offensive coordinator in Las Vegas, and was assistant offensive line coach, wide receivers coach, and quarterbacks coach during the trio of seasons (2019-21) the three were together in Minnesota. And Rick Dennison, a veteran offensive line coach who was the offensive line boss and run game coordinator in Minny for the 2019 and 2020 seasons. By The Numbers Kirk Cousins, Quarterback, 15th Year 2025: 10 games (8 starts), 166 of 269 (61.7 completion percentage), 1,721 yards, 10 touchdowns, 5 interceptions, 13 sacks, 84.8 QB rating; 14 carries, 7 yards, 1 touchdown Career: (2012-25) 174 games (167 starts), 3,934 of 5,899 (66.7 completion percentage), 44,700 yards, 298 touchdowns, 131 interceptions, 345 sacks, 96.8 QB rating; carries, 965 yards, 20 touchdowns "If you had a game tomorrow, Kirk Cousins is your best option at quarterback" @kirkmorrison with some insight into the Raiders starting QB decision 👇 pic.twitter.com/ORDoitaL1H — NFL Network (@nflnetwork) July 29, 2026 It’s a keen example of the phrase: You dance with what brung ya, meaning: You should stay loyal to the people, plans, or strategies that got you to where you are. “And that was encouraging to just see how much good football they have that they’re doing that maybe we weren’t doing four years ago or five years ago,” Cousins said of the growth he’s seen from the coaches he worked with previously. “So, that’s the way it works in this league; you just keep getting better, you keep learning new things, you keep evolving, adapting. But I came here because of who Klint and Andrew and Rick Dennison are as people, and that hasn’t changed. “And so, that’s a big encouragement for me to know that I’m with coaches that I really feel good about. That’s a big part of having success in this league.” The engrained familiarity gives Kubiak a head start on his rendition of the Raiders this season and beyond and that leg-up should portend to a feel-good story. The weight of just how long the good times roll sits squarely on the capable shoulders of Kubiak and Cousins. So let’s explore what the head coach and offensive play caller must do to get the most out of a veteran signal caller he’s worked with before. Under Center & Play-Action Centric To truly get the best out of Cousins, dialing up formations that put the heady and experienced quarterback right behind center Tyler Linderbaum to get the snap is the route Kubiak must take. Unlike how the collegiate and NFL game evolved into heavier usage of pistol and shotgun formations to give signal callers a better view to read modern defenses and escape pressure, Cousins is an old-school drop back quarterback who thrives under center due to his play-action ability and his vast pre-snap reading ability. That’s 14 seasons with the vast majority of his reps taking the direct snap under center which has made footwork, drops, and handoffs core muscle memories as Cousins heads into Year 15, and any coach that doesn’t return to those roots is going to set themselves up for failure. Unlike being deployed in pistol and shotgun formations to help him recover from injuries, Cousins heads into the 2026 campaign healthy and ready to go. And the deep familiarity with operating under center allows the quarterback to return to his natural rhythm. One of Cousins’ core strengths is hiding the ball from the defense and taking the ball directly from Linderbaum then completely turning his back to the defense for a handoff fake effectively shrouds the play in mystery and freezes defenders. Even after Cousins took over for Penix, the Falcons remained out of most pistol/shotgun heavy teams in the league. A return to an under center offense could help Cousins out tremendously. https://t.co/wLtTj61syR pic.twitter.com/cfy5NyWxyN — Ted Nguyen (@FB_FilmAnalysis) July 25, 2026 Collective Game Planning & Execution With that much equity, Cousins has no reason to be a yes man at this point in his career. And with him being so familiar with Kubiak, Cousins should have a strong voice in tailoring game plans around his strengths. Cousins excels at executing these kind of play-action fakes and is adept at spinning around, reading the field, and locating open windows downfield due to his processing of pre-snap coverages quickly. Of course, this key element goes nowhere without a consistent and established run game, so that’s where running back Ashton Jeanty and Dennison’s offensive line are integral. If the big uglies in the trenches are attune to the blocking scheme Dennison and Kubiak are installing and firing on all cylinders — ditto for Jeanty and any other tailback given the ball — the better for Cousins. Because a productive ground game opens up the play-action bootlegs and rollouts which will help Cousins attack the middle of the field in Kubiak’s air attack. We’re seeing signs of Kubiak’s ability to marry the run and pass — something he did quite well orchestrating the Seattle Seahawks Super Bowl-winning offense last season — in Las Vegas. But don’t take my word on it alone. “I think the balance of the offense. As a quarterback, this is pretty basic, but the pass is sexy,” Mendoza said after the team’s Thursday minicamp practice. “I believe that the outside zone scheme and schematics of the run that comes from the Shanahan tree is a great system, and it really complements off each other. It lets the offensive line and their talents shine. It lets the running backs and their talents shine. At the end of the day, the game is built on the run.” But Cousins’ lack of mobility and age means off-script improvisation is dampened meaning the pocket protection from the offensive line must be on point. Brock To The Future It’s no secret tight end Brock Bowers looms large for Kubiak’s offense in 2026 and beyond. A do-it-all-type who can run routes like a wide receiver but with the size of a tight end (6-foot-4 and 235 pounds) that can also block, the 23-year-old is lighting up training camp showcasing the talent that’s made him an elite player at his position after one spectacular rookie season in 2024. 🛸 Captain Kirk → Brock 🖖 #RaiderNation pic.twitter.com/5VyyQfL9kw — Las Vegas Raiders (@Raiders) July 31, 2026 If the practices thus far are any indication, Bowers is going to be heavily feature in Kubiak’s offense and Cousins has the intelligence and arm to get the talented tight end the ball frequently. Able to run crisp routes while also leaving defenders in the dust (doesn’t matter if it’s a linebacker or defensive back,…

title: Miami Dolphins Fans On The Now So-Called Green Bay Packers South
summary: I’ve noticed a recurring sentiment online describing our Miami Dolphins coaching staff as “Green Bay Packers South.” Given the theory that this influx of former Packers personnel might impact our performance in colder climates, I posed the following question this past week: Given that the Miami Dolphins train and play in the hot, humid climate […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FL - JULY 30: Miami Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley gestures as he talks to safety Dante Trader Jr. (11) during the Miami Dolphins Training Camp on July 30, 2026, at the Baptist Health Training Complex in Miami Gardens, FL. (Photo by Doug Murray/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images I’ve noticed a recurring sentiment online describing our Miami Dolphins coaching staff as “Green Bay Packers South.” Given the theory that this influx of former Packers personnel might impact our performance in colder climates, I posed the following question this past week: Given that the Miami Dolphins train and play in the hot, humid climate of South Florida, do you think the recent influx of staff from the Green Bay Packers organization will help the team overcome their struggles in cold-weather games? Will this staff be what we have needed to help level the playing field when we travel to face our division rivals in colder cities during the winter months? Below are some of your thoughts and answers- FFFL66IBA&O sees the influx of staff from Green Bay as more valuable from a cultural building standpoint. Bringing in leadership and staff with Green Bay roots (Sully & Haf etc…) brings valuable organizational culture from a cold-weather franchise, but I would think it is unlikely to instantly fix our beloved Dolphin’s physical and historical troubles playing in freezing temperatures. Sully seems to scout and draft players with rugged traits suited for all weather environments. Practicing in South Florida heat means players still experience physiological shock when stepping into sub-40-degree weather. Not so fun fact: Our beloved Dolphin’s have dropped 12 straight games when temperatures are 40 degrees or lower. In short, we need to get a Hell of a lot TOUGHER! Thank GOD we’re finally headed in the right direction…Let’s Go!!! Phoenix6 believes it will all be alright. I just don’t see this team having a problem playing & winning in NY, Blowfalo, or Boston this yr. Just dress for success… & phew! Lefty5150 points out that it’s not super realistic to expect a team in hot-humid South Florida to acclimate to very cold weather in any realistic time frame to play a game in that environment. It takes about 2-3 weeks for our bodies to adjust to weather-related temperatures. The only way to do this is to crank up the air conditioning at home and in the practice dome later in the season. Ice baths might help as well. They have to get their bodies acclimated if possible. Pod of Dolphins wanted to talk about a kid that played in Lubbock, which does get very cold at times in the winter. There is a report that Jacob Rodriguez made some nice plays on just in his first day at camp. His range in coverage was in full display Oldarmyguy believes part of adjusting to the cold is a mindset and points out that they have much better cold gear these days that the players can wear under their uniforms and pads. As a native Floridian while in the Army I was stationed in many cold places including upstate New York & Germany. It’s definitely a mind set & nowadays there’s all kind of warm weather gear comfortable enough to wear underneath uniforms. Jordan Brooks called ’em last year. He knows they wimped out. Yarganaught points out that heat or cold sucks equally for everyone. As a 4th generation Floridian who has lived in Chicago and Finland, I can say that while the cold does suck… it sucks for everyone. Same thing for the heat/humidity in Trampa or Gainesville (I lived in those cities too) during the summer. Sure, you can get acclimatized somewhat to the local temps. But when it was 108F every day in Texas, or when it was -20F in The Loop, no one was walking around outside saying “I need to get used to this!” Diggity Dankster is another who believes the key to success is getting tougher. Being from Green Bay won’t help them win in cold weather. Not being a bunch of soft wimps will. Dolfanjoe says run the ball well, play solid D, and don’t throw backward. Clearly has some leftover PTSD from Tannehill. Run game, good defensive play. Possession receivers who can block and fight for the ball. Might even think about throwing the ball downfield instead of backwards ! Ash the Elder says not much can prepare you for certain levels of cold. It’s about conditioning. Having real athletes with good cardio is one thing, but nothing prepares you for sucking in that big batch of cold air into your lungs after a hit. I don’t know if you can really practice that. Unless you spend a fortune on a refrigerated field. sdphinsfan believes the issue goes beyond cold weather to the fact that this team has overall been a poor road team in recent years. I don’t think the temperature on game day is an issue. The biggest problem is that over the last couple of decades, this team has had issues going on the road anywhere and beating a quality opponent. If you want to change that, it boils down to being able to run the ball, playing good defense, and not making stupid mistakes. And I say that not basing it on some brilliant opinion. I say it because the winningest coach in NFL history built his team to play that way. They were a warm weather team that routinely went north late in the year and dominated. JUK says I got it backwards. The question has it backwards. If you look the 10 or 15 most inportant players on this roster, 1 (Malik) is from Green Bay. What matters is the attempt to change the culture of the team. To be bigger and tougher and more professional. The guys they brought in from GB are just people they know who meet the standards of that they are looking for RW#92 says who cares about the coaches? I personally believe that while you must have good/great players, the coaching staff makes all the difference in what happens to and with those same players. Who cares about the coaches. Run the ball, play defense, and have a QB that can move the chains on 3rd down, with his legs if necessary, and you can win anywhere. SuperG! has some nuggets about the Jets. Meanwhile over in Jests land, Minkah is saying all the right things so far. However a couple of days ago Plaxico Burress dropped this bombshell on what it was like playing for the Jests. Ex-Super Bowl Champ, Who Spent Almost Two Years in Prison, Compared It to Playing for the Jets One-time Super Bowl champ Plaxico Burress did his time—both on and off the field. Back in 2009, Burress was sentenced to two years in prison for violating New York’s gun laws and pled guilty to a firearms charge that stemmed from an incident in which Burress inadvertently shot himself in the thigh at a Manhattan nightclub. Fast forward nearly two decades later, and Burress claims that his experience behind bars was similar to playing with the Jets for one season in 2011 after he was released from prison. Burress was asked during a recent appearance on Lil Wayne and Craig Carton’s The Joint Venture Show whether spending time in prison or on the Jets was worse. “So, they’re both kind of similar because when I walked into prison my first day, I was like, ‘Damn man you a f—ing loser,” Burress said, eliciting lots of laughs. “And I had the same damn feeling every day I walked through the door with the Jets. I was like, ‘Damn I hope we can win this weekend.’ Loser!” UpInPensacola points out that many of the players on the roster have experience playing in colder weather. Players are from everywhere. Many have played in cold. The franchise has been around since 1966, with Buffalo, Boston/New England, and New York always there each season. Every other team in the NFL (save dome teams) plays in cool to cold temperatures at some point. Even the I-10 corridor teams play in cool weather at times. The rest of the U.S. is not Florida. (Heck, Pensacola has had snow two winters in a row, 8 – 10 inches in ‘25! We all survived it. High school teams play in the 40’s here in late autumn, so if they can do it…) If anything, it’s warmer than it used to be, not…

title: SB Nation Reacts Results: Vikings Fans See a Return to the Postseason
summary: The results are in from our SB Nation Reacts survey for this week, ladies and gentlemen, so let’s take a look at what everyone thinks about our Minnesota Vikings topic for this week. We asked you, with training camp just having gotten underway, whether or not you feel our favorite squad will be making a […]
full_text: EAGAN, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 01: Head coach Kevin O'Connell talks to Justin Jefferson #18 of the Minnesota Vikings during Training Camp at Twin Cities Orthopedics Performance Center on August 01, 2026 in Eagan, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images The results are in from our SB Nation Reacts survey for this week, ladies and gentlemen, so let’s take a look at what everyone thinks about our Minnesota Vikings topic for this week. We asked you, with training camp just having gotten underway, whether or not you feel our favorite squad will be making a return to the postseason this year. ‘Tis, apparently, the season for positivity around here, as the local gentry feels the purple will be playing into mid-January rather than just the early portions of it. Of those who responded to our survey, a full 80% feel that the Vikings will make a return to the playoffs this season after a one-year hiatus. More of you feel that they’ll be joining the playoff field as a Wild Card team than as the NFC North division champion, with 44% of our respondents saying the Vikings will make the postseason as a Wild Card team and 36% saying they’ll win the NFC North for the first time since 2022. And there are 20% of you who responded that believe the Vikings will miss the playoffs for the second consecutive season. I do think the Vikings will make their way back to the playoffs this season, and I do think it’s more likely they’ll be there as a Wild Card than as a division champ. I expect the NFC North to, once again, be among the toughest divisions in the NFL this season, and even though the Vikings were. . .in theory. . .one botched kickoff return away from winning the NFC North last season, the margin for error is going to be pretty slim again this year. Have the Vikings made enough of the necessary changes to get over the hump and get to the top of the division? Obviously, we don’t know what role injuries are going to play around the division yet, either. Here’s hoping that our optimism isn’t misplaced when it comes to our postseason hopes for the 2026 season. We’re a little less than two weeks away from seeing an actual football game involving our favorite team, albeit one that doesn’t count for anything other than seeing who will take some of the spots at the bottom of the roster. I, for one, will just be happy to see it. As always, we want to thank all of you who took the time to participate in our survey for this week. Keep your eyes out for the next one! title: Minnesota Vikings News and Links: Paralyis by Analysis
summary: As the world turns eh? There is no escape from the incessant analyses over every rep and practice for the top two QBs on the team. Once KOC makes a decision there will be some complaining for sure but probably more so from the fans that wanted to see if JJ could be the long […]
full_text: EAGAN, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 01: Head coach Kevin O'Connell of the Minnesota Vikings looks on during Training Camp at Twin Cities Orthopedics Performance Center on August 01, 2026 in Eagan, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the world turns eh? There is no escape from the incessant analyses over every rep and practice for the top two QBs on the team. Once KOC makes a decision there will be some complaining for sure but probably more so from the fans that wanted to see if JJ could be the long term answer at QB. It is a tough situation to be in if you are KOC because you simply have not gotten enough games on tape to truly get a good idea about JJ’s future. I do not think teams can wait any longer on young QBs unless they have a purposeful plan like the Packers with Jordan Love. In that situation, they had an established starter so Love could sit and learn. The Vikings did not have that and signing Sam Darnold in 2024 was not seen as getting a starter. In turned out way better than most could have expected. Obviously everyone knows all this already. Still, I do not believe the team has abandoned or is giving up JJ in any way shape or form. They gave him the chance to compete in his first year and then gave him the job without any competition last year. They just cannot wait any longer. Even though JJ has not been able to play more, the team still has benefitted from not paying too much for the QB group overall. Even with Murray this year the team is 31st overall in cap spending on the QB group/position at $11,318,732. Last year they also were 29th $12,886,589 (includes Darnold’s 5M in dead money). In 2024, they were 6th at $40,758,418 thanks to the 28.5M dead money cap hit for Cousins. The point is that the team has been able to spend in free agency and extensions. The spending in 2025 was not ideal but I believe the deals for Allen and Hargrave were solid as evidenced by the deals they went out and got this offseason. Say what you want about Allen and Hargrave but the defense played very well especially down the stretch. It was the QB play and the offense that let the team down last year. Imagine if JJ had remained healthy all season. I believe he would have been playing better at the end of the year for sure. Maybe not a whole lot but every little bit helps. The Kelly deal is the one that hurt the most and only because he suffered the concussions. This year there were very frugal which is OK. After extending O’Neill they are sitting at $21,154,099 in cap space for 2026. Right now, the team is sitting at $29,932,787 in cap space for 2027 (according to overthecap) but it does not include the 12M in cap credits they will get from Allen and Hargrave signing pretty similar deals in free agency this offseason. After adding in the 12M, the Vikings will have roughly 41.93M in cap space for 2027 before adding in any carryover from this year and doing extensions (Van Giunkel, Cashman, Mason, and maybe Hockenson) or cuts (Metellus, Fries, Theo Jackson, and Tavierre Thomas offer decent savings). It is going to be interesting to see what the new GM and his team envision. But, I digress. I am supposed to be talking about the QB competition. I really cannot put a lot of stock into how these two do every single day. They both could be up and down at times even in the same practice. I have already stated how I think it is going to go as well. I believe they want Murray to start. Simple as that. What that means for JJ is anyone’s guess. 2026 Vikings Training Camp Full Schedule https://www.vikings.com/schedule/vikings-events/training-camp/schedule DATE : TIME : PRACTICE Saturday, Aug. 1 : Noon- 5 p.m. : 2:30 p.m. Monday, Aug. 3 : Noon – 5 p.m. : 2:30 p.m. Tuesday, Aug. 4 : Noon – 5 p.m. : 2:30 p.m. Wednesday, Aug. 5 : Noon – 5 p.m. : 2:30 p.m. Friday, Aug. 7 : Noon – 5 p.m. : 2:30 p.m. Saturday, Aug. 8 : Noon – 5 p.m. : 2:30 p.m. Sunday, Aug. 9 : 5 – 11 p.m. : 7 p.m. Tuesday, Aug. 11 : Noon – 5 p.m. : 2:30 p.m. Wednesday, Aug. 12 : Noon – 5 p.m. : 2:30 p.m. Thursday, Aug. 13 : Noon – 5 p.m. : 2:30 p.m. Monday, Aug. 17 : Noon – 5 p.m. : 2:30 p.m. Wednesday, Aug. 19 : Noon – 5 p.m. : 2:30 p.m. : Joint Practice with Baltimore Ravens Thursday, Aug. 20 : Noon – 5 p.m. : 2:30 p.m. : Joint Practice with Baltimore Ravens The Minnesota Vikings 2026 preseason schedule features three matchups Week 1: Saturday, August 15 at New York Giants (1:00 PM ET) Week 2: Saturday, August 22 vs. Baltimore Ravens (12:00 PM ET) Week 3: Friday, August 28 at Denver Broncos (Time TBD) Minnesota Vikings News and Links Vikings training camp recap, Day 4: Kyler Murray bounces back in a big way https://bringmethesports.com/vikings-training-camp-recap-day-4-kyler-murray-bounces-back-in-a-big-way Over the first two days of Vikings training camp, it was perhaps fair to give a slight edge to J.J. McCarthy in the team’s quarterback competition. He took what the defense gave him and stacked completions, while Kyler Murray had some predictable ups and downs as he continues to get acclimated in a new offense. Thursday wasn’t great for Murray. That was not the case on Saturday. In the team’s third full-speed practice of camp (and fourth overall), Murray was the clear winner of the QB battle. He looked comfortable and played like a guy who has started almost 100 games in the NFL. McCarthy, meanwhile, looked quite a bit shakier than he did in the first couple days. Murray’s sharp day Murray’s very first dropback in 11-on-11 set the tone for what kind of day he would go on to have. With Jordan Addison running a clearout deep route up the right side, Murray waited and fired a perfect ball to Justin Jefferson, who was running a deep crosser into the space underneath Addison’s route. It’s the exact kind of play that has been a staple of Kevin O’Connell’s offense and Jefferson’s game. Later in the opening period of 11s, Murray made another great anticipatory throw to Myles Price, who found a small window of space beyond the linebackers. Price couldn’t quite complete the catch. The Vikings did their 7-on-7 work in the low red zone in this practice. After checking down to Aaron Jones on his first rep, Murray fired one over the middle for a touchdown to T.J. Hockenson. He nearly found Hockenson for another TD towards the right pylon, but the Vikings’ top tight end lost the ball in the process of trying to complete a lunging catch. Murray then progressed through his options and went underneath to Zavier Scott for a score. Back in 11-on-11, Murray threw a slant to Jefferson in stride, then found his top receiver in open space again. Murray and Jefferson connected five times in this practice, by my count. Their rapport seems to be picking up already. As the cherry on top of Murray’s day, he ended with a nice intermediate throw up the seam to Tai Felton, who was covered tightly but was able to make the grab. It’s still very early, of course. But this was the type of day where you could really see the upside with Murray in O’Connell’s offense, throwing to Jefferson and these other weapons. McCarthy struggles Murray played well enough on Saturday that he was going to be hard to “beat” if evaluating each day of the competition as its own mini battle. But McCarthy didn’t even make it close. This was his least effective day of the three so far. McCarthy’s first throw was a checkdown that was tipped at the line and incomplete. He then sailed a ball that was intended for Jauan Jennings in tight coverage towards the left sideline. And to wrap up his first bundle of 11-on-11 reps, McCarthy had a pass tipped by rookie linebacker Jake Golday that was picked off by Blake Cashman. In red zone 7s, McCarthy’s first attempt for Tai Felton was broken up by Charles Demmings. On the next one, he held onto the ball for a long time before rolling out and throwing to nobody. McCarthy did connect with Gavin Bartholomew and Dillon Bell for touchdowns, sandwiched around a high throw for Felton in the back of the end…

title: Patriots training camp competitions, updated heading into second week
summary: The New England Patriots’ training camp is in full swing, which means that the race for roster spots is starting to heat up as well. A total of 53 are available, and with a significant chunk of those already allocated to players such as Drake Maye, A.J. Brown, Milton Williams or Christian Gonzalez, only a […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - MAY 27: Tommy DeVito #16 of the New England Patriots gives th ball to Jam Miller #30 of the New England Patriots during New England Patriots OTA on May 27, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. Sportswire) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots’ training camp is in full swing, which means that the race for roster spots is starting to heat up as well. A total of 53 are available, and with a significant chunk of those already allocated to players such as Drake Maye, A.J. Brown, Milton Williams or Christian Gonzalez, only a handful effectively remains up for competition. With the eighth practice of the summer set to take place on Monday, and with three full-pads practices now in the books, let’s update our rundown of camp competitions to see if we can find any trends. Patriots camp competition update: August 3 Quarterback: The quarterback pecking order itself has not changed, with Drake Maye undisputed at the top and Tommy DeVito and Behren Morton filling the second and third spots, respectively. That said, Morton is getting a significant number of reps and continued to show some encouraging moments since the introduction of full pads. He certainly is no shoo-in for the chopping block, far from it actually. Running back: While he remains third on the provisional depth chart, Lan Larison has not shown the same consistency and big play ability as rookie Jam Miller. Based on their trajectory throughout camp, Miller now looks like the favorite for the top spot behind Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson. Wide receiver: After a slow start to his second NFL training camp, Kyle Williams has picked up the pace lately. He still has not seen regular targets from Drake Maye and the top offense, but the arrow is pointing up. Kayshon Boutte, meanwhile, has been quiet after his fast start to camp. That said, his chemistry with Drake Maye remains one of the best on the team and still shines through regularly. Among the undrafted wideouts, Cameron Dorner looks like the best of the bunch, but making a roster currently headlined by A.J. Brown, Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas, Boutte, Mack Hollins, Williams and Efton Chism will still be next to impossible. Tight end: Hunter Henry is the No. 1, Eli Raridon is the No. 2, and Tanner Arkin is the No. 3. That was the pecking order before padded practices, and nothing has changed since. If anything, the undrafted rookie Arkin has only strengthened his hold of a roster spot. He’s the best blocking tight end the Patriots have. Offensive tackle: The top trio of Will Campbell, Morgan Moses and Caleb Lomu remains undisputed. A potential fourth spot behind still seems to be the subject of a head-to-head competition between Marcus Bryant and James Hudson. The latter suffered an undisclosed injury during Saturday’s practice. Interior offensive line: The introduction of full pads saw a change along the backup interior line. Third-year man Caedan Wallace lost his spot as one of the second-string guards to Mehki Butler, and to make matter worse was also injured on Saturday. At the moment, the interior backups are led by Ben Brown and Andrew Rupcich, with second-year man Butler now also part of the mix. Interior defensive line: No dramatic changes on the interior defensive line. Milton Williams and Christian Barmore are the clear starers, with Cory Durden rotating in and out with the first-stringers. The other depth spots belong to Joshua Farmer and Leonard Taylor, who both had flashes but have not been overly consistent. No serious push has come from the rest of the DT group, despite Eric Gregory having a few positive moments. Defensive edge: Gabe Jacas’ return is obviously good news for the group, even as Harold Landry remains sidelined. The second-round draft pick has yet to show what he is capable of — he remains a limited practice participant — but he will take a spot in the rotation at some point. This, in turn, might lead to Elijah Ponder seeing a reduction in starter reps opposite Dre’Mont Jones. Elsewhere, Bradyn Swinson is mostly a reserve option but showing some pass rushing skill. Xavier Holmes, another UDFA making some noise, has not sustained his earlier momentum and could see the quality of his reps decrease with Jacas now in the fold as well. Linebacker: Khalil Jacobs is pushing for a roster spot. The undrafted rookie has started stringing good days together and accordingly could be coming for K.J. Britt and Chad Muma, who are still the top backup linebackers right now. None of their spots are chiseled in stone, however, meaning that Jacobs very well could end up overtaking at least one them at some point. Special teams might end up a deciding factor, which is also where rookie Namdi Obiazor has played most of his meaningful reps. Cornerback: Carlton Davis’ recent absence has opened the door for Charles Woods to regularly rep with the starters; it is clear that he is the current CB4 behind Christian Gonzalez, Davis and Marcus Jones. The fifth and sixth spots might be coming down to one or two of Kindle Vildor, Karon Prunty, Kobee Minor and Marcellas Dial Jr. Minor, however, has had some rough stretches of play particularly on Thursday and Friday. He needs to overcome those if he wants to remain in the competition. Safety: Dell Pettus, take a bow. The third-year safety registered an interception on Saturday, and appears to be hitting his stride. The same cannot be said for Mike Brown, who is his primary competition for the third safety spot but has had some ups and downs over the last few sessions. John Saunders Jr, who also filled the third spot at one point, has primarily been on special teams and third-string duty. Special teams: Nothing has changed in the kicking game. Andy Borregales, Bryce Baringer and Julian Ashby have no competition on the roster, while Marcus Jones is still the top punt returner. In the kickoff return game, meanwhile, Kyle Williams and Lan Larison have been the top two. The Patriots are scheduled to hold five straight practices this week, starting on Monday. For more info, please check out our Pats Pulpit Training Camp Guide .
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Sunday Patriots Notes: Eli Raridon impressing early in training camp
summary: The New England Patriots’ training camp is fully underway. Following three straight padded practices to conclude the first week, the team is off on Sunday before getting back to work. Before we focus on what lies ahead, however, let’s take one final look back at the week that was. Welcome to the latest installment of […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA- JUNE 11: Eli Raridon #82 of the New England Patriots speaks to the media after New England Patriots Minicamp on June 11, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Summer Lamont/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots’ training camp is fully underway. Following three straight padded practices to conclude the first week, the team is off on Sunday before getting back to work. Before we focus on what lies ahead, however, let’s take one final look back at the week that was. Welcome to the latest installment of our Sunday Patriots Notes . Raridon’s hot start Through seven training camp practices, it’s been hard to miss rookie tight end Eli Raridon. Raridon has been active as a pass catcher this summer, often threatening New England’s up the seam and running away from second-level defenders across the field. On Friday, that led to the rookie catching multiple passes during 7-on-7s, including a touchdown in the corner of the end zone from Drake Maye — a unit he is regularly been apart of as the team’s No. 2 tight end. “He is a big dude, first off, that can run. I mean, that’s pretty cool, and he is smart,” Maye said. “He went to Notre Dame and I know he is another guy that, half ACC, half not, but we like to call ourselves smart in the ACC so— He understands positions, he understands how to play both positions, the tight end spot. I think he is making plays on the football. That’s what you want to see from a young guy, and he is putting the work in. “That is the biggest thing with a young rookie. You want to see him go out there and take a rep when he is tired and not call for a sub, and he is doing all the things the right way, and I am looking forward to seeing what he does throughout camp. He has been a great player for us and a great dude.” While Raridon has seen his fair share of reps with Maye and the first-team offense, the rookie remains slotted behind veteran Hunter Henry on the depth chart. That has also led to plenty of work with backup quarterback Tommy DeVito, who has no issues peppering the tight end with targets. “Have you seen him? That’s a big target. I bet you’d want to throw to him too,” DeVito said. “I mean, he’s big, he’s athletic, his confidence is growing. Trying to get more savvy with the offense, like as it’s going. But that just comes with time and how many reps he gets. So, just keep trying to get as many reps as we can. I know he’s got a lot of information coming at him. I know I’ve been a rookie before in a situation like this. So just keep him encouraged, keep him going. But he’s got awesome hands, he’s got the frame. He’s got everything going for him. So, I’m looking forward to seeing how he plays this year.” A quiet spring from Raridon, coupled with a season-ending injury to veteran free-agent addition Julian Hill, left the door open for a potential free agent addition at the position. While there is still work to be done for the 2026 third-round pick, Raridon’s emergence early in camp has him trending toward earning a role as a rookie. “You can see the game slowing down for him a little bit,” Hunter Henry said. “Every single time he gets reps, he learns from those reps. He’s watching them in the film room. We’re talking about things. He’s got a bright future ahead of him for sure.” CB depth The Patriots depth at cornerback has been tested early in camp with Carlton Davis (unknown) sidelined for the last three practices after leaving Tuesday’s session early. Charles Woods has consistently been first up in his place. “Just having a full offseason in the system now, I’m more comfortable with the play calling. I’m understanding the scheme, what we’re trying to get done as a defense, and now just going out there and playing football,” said Woods, who spent last season as the No. 4 cornerback after being claimed off waivers during cutdown day. With Christian Gonzalez (rest) then limited on Saturday, Kobee Minor, Kindle Vildor, and fifth-round pick Karon Prunty saw elevated snaps. Prunty made the most of it with an interception off of DeVito while Minor also recorded a pass breakup. That group will continue to sort itself out over the next few weeks with roster spots limited. Gonzo update Beyond being a limited participant on Saturday due to rest reasons, Christian Gonzalez has remained a full participant in padded practices as he searches for a contract extension. Mike Vrabel has appreciated that approach from his top cornerback this offseason, but did not have an update on where negotiations stood. “It’ll either get done, and when it gets done, that’ll be the progress that’s made,” Vrabel said Saturday. “Everybody that’s involved is working hard. I cannot express the professionalism that Gonzo has started camp with. It’s clear that he wants to improve, that he wants to be the best at his craft and at that position. I think that he’s made that known by the way he’s come out here to practice.” Underrated names Training camp always provides a chance for underrated players to make a push for roster spots. Through seven practices, here are some who have caught our eyes: RB Jam Miller: While New England’s defensive front has largely won the rushing periods, Miller has caught the eye on numerous occasions for his quickness and ability to find holes. Lan Larison still seems like the top RB3, but Miller could make a push. WR Cameron Dorner: Dorner has been stacking positive days together which was recently rewarded with a handful of reps with Tommy DeVito and the second string offense. The UDFA receiver has shown the ability to separate and while the wide receiver depth chart is crowded, New England lost practice squader Jeremiah Webb for the season. Dorner is making an early case to stick around in that capacity. TE Tanner Arkin: Perhaps no longer underrated as the UDFA has consistently seen time with the top offense due to his blocking ability. That ability has slotted him in nicely behind Hunter Henry and Eli Raridon, and Arkin’s blocking ability has created some short play-action opportunities through the air. LB Khalil Jacobs: On the defensive side of the ball, Jacobs has repped next to K.J. Britt and Chad Muma recently on the second team defense. He logged a pressure in Saturday’s practice and has been around the ball often in run defense from the off-ball linebacker spot. Chism’s growth Efton Chism and Mack Hollins quickly developed a strong relationship during Chism’s rookie season as they would often be two of the first people in the facility. The two enjoy pushing each other to get better and Chism calls Hollins one of his best friends, but the veteran has enjoyed seeing the 24-year old’s growth in Year 2. “I think the biggest thing is now he’s taken anything that he was with me doing last year, and he’s molded it. And like I told him, take everything I do, and then change to what’s best for you. And that’s what I’ve seen him do,” Hollins said. “It’s been it’s been really cool to watch him grow not only as a player on the field, but off in understanding how to be a pro and things it takes to be great and sustain that for more than a season and not just be like, ‘Oh, it’s a guy that is shining in a training camp for one year cause he’s small and white.’ Efton’s a baller, that’s why he’s shining.” WR room Chism will have work to do to make the 53-man roster again this season after the team added A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs to pair with him and Mack Hollins, Kyle Williams, DeMario Douglas, and Kayshon Boutte. Keeping all seven wide receivers on the Week 1 roster feels like a stretch, which means one will be the odd man out. That could be still be Kayshon Boutte, who remains open to a trade after requesting one back in the spring, which would open the door for youngsters like Chism and Kyle Williams, who would remain a surprise cut, to remain off waivers. “I love having depth, but I would say that we’re always going to try to look to…

summary: Throughout the New Orleans Saints roster, there are heated position battles that are difficult to predict. The top of that list is the wide receivers group. New Orleans put so much effort into upgrading that unit, and with Jordyn Tyson, Chris Olave, Devaughn Vele, Bryce Lance, and Barion Brown a part of that group, only […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 24: JaÕLynn Polk #1 of the New England Patriots stands on the sidelines during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium on November 24, 2024 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Throughout the New Orleans Saints roster, there are heated position battles that are difficult to predict. The top of that list is the wide receivers group. New Orleans put so much effort into upgrading that unit, and with Jordyn Tyson, Chris Olave, Devaughn Vele, Bryce Lance, and Barion Brown a part of that group, only one spot likely remains for the other WRs on the roster. The person who led that battle was WR Ja’Lynn Polk. The former second-round pick with the New England Patriots never found his footing on his first team, and struggles plagued his first season. Unfortunately, he was injured before year 2 could start and was ruled out for the entire season, however the Saints still took a gamble on him and made a trade which included a 7th-rounder and Polk for a 6th-rounder. Even when injured, Polk made sure to create chemistry with his potential future QBs, including Tyler Shough. With his talent coming out of college and the chemistry he built, Polk chould have won the WR battle, but there’s a reason I say chould have. Today, the Saints announced that Polk was placed on the reserve/retiring list, which means the young WR’s career in the NFL is over. The #Saints have placed WR Ja’Lynn Polk on reserve/retired list — Tina Howell (@TinaM_Howell) August 2, 2026 This announcement very unexpected. As I mentioned, Polk was the favorite and has been present for most of the practices. He was out for personal reasons during the last 2 days, which could have led up to his decision to retire from the league. As of now, those reasons are unknown. Regarding the WR battle, this news changes everything. Now, that last remaining spot is wide open, and players like Brock Rechsteiner, Mason Tipton, Ronnie Bell, Trey Palmer, Jalen Moreno-Cropper, Kevin Austin Jr., and Bub Means have a clearer path to winning it. But there are still way too many players involved in this competition to choose a potential winner.

title: NY Giants 53-man roster projection, Week 1 update: Locks, bubble players, long shots
summary: Instead of doing a pure 53-man roster projection ahead of New York Giants training camp, we are looking at the Giants’ 91-man roster a different way Below is an updated position-by-position look at who I consider to be locks to make the 53-man roster, bubble players, and long shots after the first four days of […]
full_text: Odell Beckham | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Instead of doing a pure 53-man roster projection ahead of New York Giants training camp, we are looking at the Giants’ 91-man roster a different way Below is an updated position-by-position look at who I consider to be locks to make the 53-man roster, bubble players, and long shots after the first four days of practice. The intent is to look at where the most interesting competitions are and the chances of individual players. Quarterback Locks (2) — Jaxson Dart, Jameis Winston Bubble players (0) — None Long shot (1) — Brandon Allen [No change] Allen received few reps over the first four days. The Giants did one 7-on-7 session in each of those practices, and Dart often took Allen’s reps with the third team. As coach John Harbaugh said in the spring, whatever reps Dart wants, Dart will get. Running back Locks (4) — Cam Skattebo, Tyrone Tracy, Devin Singletary, Patrick Ricard Bubble players (1) — Dante Miller Long shots (3) — Eric Gray, Damon Bankston [ Change: Miller moves from long shot to bubble] At the risk of getting the ‘Turbo-maniacs’ fired up, only to once again end up disappointed, it has been clear through the early practices that the Giants see Miller as being ahead of Gray or Bankston. I still won’t believe Miller will make the roster until I see it happen. Tight end Locks (3) — Isaiah Likely, Theo Johnson, Chris Manhertz Bubble players (1) — Tanner Conner Long shot (1) — Thomas Fidone [ Change: Conner and Fidone switch places] Conner has made plays every day. Fidone, coming back from foot issues, has been mostly invisible. Wide receiver Locks (5) — Malik Nabers, Darius Slayton, Calvin Austin, Darnell Mooney, Malachi Fields Bubble players (4) — Odell Beckham Jr., JuJu Smith-Schuster, Braxton Berrios, Dalen Cambre Long shots (5) — Ryan Miller, Jalin Hyatt, Xavier Gipson, Beaux Collins, Isaiah Hodgins [ Change: Cambre and Hodgins switch places] I still don’t have a good handle on who leads the competition for the last roster spot or two at this position. Berrios had a good start to camp. Beckham hasn’t done much, but he has practiced every day. I switched Cambre and Hodgins because of special teams value. Offensive line Locks (7) — Andrew Thomas, Jon Runyan, John Michael Schmitz, Francis Mauigoa, Jermaine Eluemunor, Marcus Mbow, Daniel Faalele Bubble players (6) — J.C. Davis, Lucas Patrick, Bryan Hudson, Josh Ezeudu, Aaron Stinnie Long shots (4) — Evan Neal, Ryan Schernecke, Jake Kubas, Jarrod Gray (International Exemption) [ Change: Runyan moved from bubble to lock.] There was no indication over the first four practices that Runyan is in a competition for the starting left guard job. Defensive line Locks (4) — D.J. Reader, Darius Alexander, Shelby Harris, Chauncey Golston Bubble players (5) — Bobby Jamison-Travis, Leki Fotu, Zacch Pickens, Sam Roberts, Josh Tupou Long shots (2) — Anquin Barnes Jr., Marlon Davidson [ Change: Undrafted free agent Ben Barten was cut; Davidson was added to the roster to replace C.J. Ravenell] Padded practices begin on Monday. That should be when this competition begins to declare itself. Off-ball linebacker Locks (3) — Arvell Reese, Tremaine Edmunds, Micah McFadden Bubble players (3) — Jack Kelly, Darius Muasau, Zaire Barnes Long shots (1) — Anfernee Orji [ Change: Orji added to roster] Orji was signed to replace Barten. Kelly is edging closer to becoming a lock. One other note: Harbaugh said last week that he considered McFadden a third starter. Edge defender Locks (3) — Brian Burns, Abdul Carter, Kayvon Thibodeaux Bubble players (1) — Khalid Kareem Long shots (2) — Trace Ford, Caleb Murphy [No change] I still see only the three edge defenders making the 53-man roster. Cornerback Locks (5) — Paulson Adebo, Greg Newsome II, Colton Hood, Dru Phillips, Deonte Banks Bubble players (3) — Art Green, Nic Jones, Korie Black Long shots (1) — Jarick Bernard-Converse [C hange: Banks moved bubble to lock.] Banks is now where I probably should have put him initially. Safety Locks (3) — Jevon Holland, Tyler Nubin, Ar’Darius Washington Bubble players (2) — Elijah Campbell, Jason Pinnock Long shots (2) — Beau Brade, Raheem Layne [No change] The more I watch practice, the more I believe Washington is going to play a lot. Special teams Locks (1) — Jordan Stout (punter) Bubble players (2) — Dominic Zvada (placekicker), Ben Mann (long-snapper) Long shot (1) — Ben Sauls (placekicker) [No change] I do believe Sauls has a chance to win the placekicking job. I still think Zvada is the front runner. Totals Locks: 40 Bubble players: 28 Long shots: 23

title: ‘Kudos & Wet Willies’ after 4 days of NY Giants training camp
summary: WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — With the New York Giants enjoying their first off day of training camp, let’s assess the first four days in our traditional “Kudos & Wet Willies” style. Kudos The beautiful setting — This is a gorgeous place. If you love lush green trees, the mountains, open spaces, fresh air with […]
full_text: WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — With the New York Giants enjoying their first off day of training camp, let’s assess the first four days in our traditional “Kudos & Wet Willies” style. Kudos The beautiful setting — This is a gorgeous place. If you love lush green trees, the mountains, open spaces, fresh air with a lack of humidity, crisp evenings and early mornings, and the feel of having stepped back in time to an earlier era this is the kind of place for you. Kayvon Thibodeaux — Thibodeaux has taken more reps with the second team than the first team, but no matter. He is a key part of the defense and is being used both on the edge and at times in the old Justin Tuck role as an interior pass rusher. Thibodeaux has made impact plays every day against starters and backups. He seems happy, and could be primed for a big season in his contract year. Abdul Carter — The second-year edge defender has been impactful throughout the first four practices. Of course, Andrew Thomas and the other offensive linemen are not in pads, making it more difficult to block. Carter might not win Defensive Player of the Year , but he does seem primed to make a big leap in Year 2. Braxton Berrios — The veteran wide receiver/return man keeps showing up as a receiver. He has made a number of catches each day. It is early in camp, but Berrios is showing he can be a useful player. Calvin Austin — I don’t know how much the diminutive slot receiver is going to play on offense, but he has been showing the ability to get open and make some plays down the field. Arvell Reese/Tremaine Edmunds — When the Giants drafted Reese No. 5 overall, they were excited about how the size and athleticism of the duo of inside linebackers could impact the passing game in the middle of the field. We have seen that manifest over the first four practices with interceptions, batted passes, and with Jaxson Dart carefully trying to float passes over them. The pace of practice — I love the way the Giants are practicing. After special teams and individual work at the beginning of practice, the remainder of the work each day has been 11-on-11 or 7-on-7 at a brisk pace. No walk-through breaks. No special teams periods designed to give frontline players a break. Each 11-on-11 period has a different purpose, or simulates a different situation. Players are shuttled in and out quickly so they don’t get overworked. “Practice has been at a great pace, but I feel like, again, we’ve done such a good job of mixing and matching guys that it allows for people to be able to play fast and play hard,” Darius Slayton said. “Ultimately, you stack more explosive reps. You don’t get into as many of those, six or seven, eight reps in a row, the reality is by the time you get seven, eight reps in, you’re fried. I definitely think that’s been great.” The placekicking competition — There is nothing easier to track than a placekicking competition. All you have to do is count the makes and misses, and track distances the best you can. Dominic Zvada and Ben Sauls are alternating days kicking, and they are basically having a “what you can do I can do better” competition. Both have kicked well, and have made kicks from beyond 55 yards. I believe Zvada has the edge, but I also think both of these guys are going to kick in the NFL for a while. Sauls seems to have fixed whatever issue caused him to struggle in the spring. It’s been fun to watch them compete. Wet Willies The Greenbrier Turf Field — The Greenbrier Sports Performance Center is billed as having two grass fields and a turf field. Well, it does have a turf field. Except it isn’t really usable, or accessible. It’s carved into the side of a mountain off to the side and a few hundred feet below the two grass fields. Getting there was described to me as “dangerous”, and I have no idea how to do so. The Giants won’t be using it. Oh, the only other football-related drawback to being at the Greenbrier. There is no indoor practice bubble. It is supposed to rain for much of the upcoming week in West Virginia. The Giants will have to practice on the grass in the rain. Not ideal. No tweeting during practice — Honestly, not tweeting during practice — and the strict limits on when photos and videos can be taken — makes my life easier. I can simply focus on what is happening on the field. Still, it stinks for fans who are starving for practice news, highlights, and info. It will also stink in the event something like a big injury happens, and we can’t tell you about it in real-time.

title: Darius Slayton got what he wanted, and loves what John Harbaugh brings to the Giants
summary: WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — At the end of the 2025 season, New York Giants wide receiver Darius Slayton told media that he hoped the team would hire a Coughlin-esque head coach. The Giants, of course, hired John Harbaugh, an old-school coach with a Super Bowl title and an 18-year track record filled with success. […]
full_text: Darius Slayton | Getty Images WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — At the end of the 2025 season, New York Giants wide receiver Darius Slayton told media that he hoped the team would hire a Coughlin-esque head coach. The Giants, of course, hired John Harbaugh , an old-school coach with a Super Bowl title and an 18-year track record filled with success. So, did Slayton get what he wanted? “I would say so,” Slayton told assembled media at The Greenbrier Sports Performance Center on Friday. “Yeah, absolutely. I feel like he’s in that echelon, that ilk. He obviously came from arguably one of the most old-school divisions in football of the Ravens and the Steelers. I definitely think he’s what we needed. There’s definitely been a sense of accountability off the rip, which has been huge for us. I’m definitely glad Coach Harbaugh’s here.” Slayton did not want to give specific examples of Harbaugh holding anyone accountable. That was a veteran move, smartly not throwing any teammates under the bus. He spoke in general terms. “Already in this camp, he’s already kind of expressed that at the end of the day, in this life, if somebody’s not doing something up to the echelon that you want them to do, you go to them, you make that clear to them that that’s not what we’re going to do around here, then they have a chance to respond,” Slayton said. “And that’s something that he’s already done in our first few days of camp and has gotten a positive response out of the individuals that he’s done that with. So, I think that’s really big for a football team.” ‘I need to be able to run’ Slayton missed spring practices after having offseason surgery for a double sports hernia. He admitted that last season, when he had the second-lowest production of his seven-year NFL career, he played through the issue. “I pretty much started with it last season, and just kind of played that way throughout the whole season,” he said. “Just because I wasn’t going to just cut the season short with the surgery or anything. I got through last year, and then I tried to kind of rehab it in the offseason, and it just didn’t really work. So, I just went ahead and got the procedure done.” Slayton admitted that the hernias had “a good bit” of impact on his season. “I’m not a big excuse person. So, at the end of the day, I could have played better regardless, but obviously it’s different when maybe you’re used to being able to catch the ball a little easier,” Slayton said. “You’re having to strain a little more and maybe come up an inch short here or there. But at the end of the day, if you’re out there, you’ve got to make it happen.” Slayton has had a quiet start to training camp, but he has been on the field taking a full complement of reps every day. “I need to be able to run. I need to be able to move how I’m accustomed to being able to move,” Slayton said. “Honestly, once that’s all done, I believe I’ll play to a level that I need to play at.” ‘The old guy role’ The trade of Dexter Lawrence to the Cincinnati Bengals left the 29-year-old Slayton, a fifth-round pick in the 2019 NFL Draft, as the longest-tenured Giant. “Everybody keeps trying to fit me in the old guy role,” Slayton said. “But you know Odell’s [Beckham] older than me, Braxton’s [Berrios] older than me, JuJu’s [Smith-Schuster] the same age as me,” Slayton said. “So, I’m trying to shake that narrative. But, no, other than that, I feel like I’ve always just kind of been a glue guy. Kind of a do-it-all guy. There’s not really too much for a receiver position that I’m not capable of doing. My plan is to fill whatever holes need to be filled and be successful at my role.” Slayton has made a career out of exceeding expectations and always becoming a key part of the Giants’ offense. It won’t be a surprise if he does it again.

title: Sean Mannion sets Eagles training camp expectations, talks Jalen Hurts, and more
summary: The Eagles were back on the practice field on Saturday, but before taking the field, new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion spoke to reporters — in just his second time speaking to Philly media since being hired. He explained his training camp expectations, why he’s enjoyed working with Jalen Hurts, and their approaches to installing a […]
full_text: The Eagles were back on the practice field on Saturday, but before taking the field, new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion spoke to reporters — in just his second time speaking to Philly media since being hired. He explained his training camp expectations, why he’s enjoyed working with Jalen Hurts, and their approaches to installing a new offensive scheme. Here’s what the OC had to say: On Jalen Hurts “He’s very uniquely talented in terms of that athletic ability, it’s something he’s been effective with throughout his career. So, that’s part of what makes him such a special talent, but he does a lot of things well. I think he’s really operated through all facets of the offense comfortably, but the piece of him as an athlete in the running game that is unique. Those are elements we can lean in to, as well.” Mannion had a lot of good things to say about working with Hurts since getting to Philadelphia, and noted that the QB has had a lot of success and played in a lot of games, so his goal to get a feel for what he likes. That includes finding Hurts’ comfort calls, what he feels super confident with in a 2nd-and-long situation, and those nuanced details will help the OC as a play-caller. “It’s been a great partnership with Jalen [Hurts] since we got here. The back and forth has been outstanding, he asks really thought-provoking questions, and it’s been a lot of fun to work with him” On training camp expectations “The thing we want is great effort every day, and then compete. That was a big thing coming into this camp for us, was every day is high-level competition — you’re competing against yourself, competing for a role on the roster, and then competing against the defense every day is going to make us better and better.” Mannion went on to explain that offensively, they’re looking at whether they have a tight pre-snap operation — something the OC admitted they struggled with in Day 1 of camp, but thought things were improved Day 2. “And then just, assignment, alignment, execution — are we getting lined up properly? Are we not having mental errors? But, through the first two days of practice, it’s still early, I’m happy with the progress we’ve made, and we just gotta keep improving from there.” The OC later said that the more veteran guys have been great and super willing to learn a new system. He noted that the biggest thing is that all of the guys are so hungry to learn and for individual periods when they’re working on technique. “Those are the type of guys you get to work with every day. Again, from the offseason program, you know, you have a summer break, and coming back, I thought Day 1 and 2, there was some pre-snap stuff we need to fix, but their retention from the spring was outstanding. And it allows us to pick up right where we left off and kind of keep building from there.” On the WR room Mannion said that they have a very exciting group of players at wide receiver with such complimentary skillsets. They have a lot of flexibility with being able to put guys at different spots and move people around, which opens up a lot of opportunities. On the new scheme Mannion didn’t want to get too deep into what they’re planning to do schematically, but did say that guys like Saquon Barkley and Tank Bigsby are certainly capable of being utilized out of the backfield. He noted that the running backs sometimes have blocking duties, or other things based on what the defense is doing, but they are all capable pass catchers and good route runners that can be used based on protection needs. When asked if he wants a true fullback in the offense, the OC explained their overall approach to these kind of schematic details. “As multiple as we can be formationally, I think that’s always something we want to try to do. And especially train these guys to do multiple things throughout camp.” Lane Johnson and Jordan Mailata had mentioned earlier in the week that the scheme is easier for them upfront, and Mannion said that the coaches are focused on making things as simple for them as possible — in addition to some things with the tight ends that provides more support than they’ve had previously. “We want these guys to go out there, know exactly where to go, and play fast. So, throughout all of our teaching, we want to make as many things as black and white for them as possible, so we’re all on the same page and we’re off and running. At least we all know where we’re going, and we’re going with total assignment commitment to attack our aiming points, attack our targets, and that will ultimately allow us to play fast, play physical, have the play style that we want. But, we want to make everything as cut and dry, and black and white for the offensive line so they can fire off.“ Other notables The OC said he was really impressed with the recall and retention that everyone had coming back from summer break. He said that they were clearly studying during the time away. Mannion called the Eagles defense under DC Vic Fangio a “tremendous group” and it makes great competition for the offense every day going against an elite unit — the OC said it was a bit of a daily chess match. He talked about how much he enjoys spending time with all the different positions, and acknowledged he has to be a little more intentional with him time. Mannion said he finds extra time with the QBs, and sometimes OL, when the rest of the group is in special teams meetings.

title: Eagles News: Hoping to see more from Philadelphia’s top two draft picks
summary: Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Eagles 2026 training camp practice notes, Day 3: The D-line is dominant – PhillyVoiceIt’s very early in camp, but I haven’t seen Eli Stowers or Makai Lemon do anything impressive so far. Hurts fired a deep ball to Lemon today, but he was pretty easily […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JULY 30: Makai Lemon #9 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on during training camp at Jefferson Health Training Complex on July 30, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Eagles 2026 training camp practice notes, Day 3: The D-line is dominant – PhillyVoice It’s very early in camp, but I haven’t seen Eli Stowers or Makai Lemon do anything impressive so far. Hurts fired a deep ball to Lemon today, but he was pretty easily blanketed by Cooper DeJean and the pass fell incomplete. One note on Stowers is that he was working on blocking with the offensive line while other tight ends like Dallas Goedert, Johnny Mundt, Grant Calcaterra, and Cameron Latu were doing route-runner drills with the quarterbacks. That makes sense, since blocking is the more underdeveloped part of his game. Eagles Training Camp Practice Notes: Jalyx Hunt and Jalen Carter help defense win the day – BGN SLOW START FOR THE EAGLES’ TOP TWO DRAFT PICKS: All the necessary disclaimers apply here. Rookie players, only the third day of camp, no pads yet, new offense going up against an established defense, yada yada yada. So, we’re in a safe space now, right? No one is going to overreact to what I’m about to share? Okay, good … because it’s been a quiet start to camp for Makai Lemon and Eli Stowers. (gasp) Camp Notes – Big Day for the D – Iggles Blitz Lemon is a work in progress. He has the skills to be a good slot receiver right away, but there is a new scheme and he’s facing one of the best defenses in the league. That can make things tough on a rookie. It will be interesting to see him develop as camp progresses. Eagles practice observations: Makai Lemon feels it; Jalen Carter dominates; how much will Jalen Hurts run? – Inquirer Makai Lemon was targeted more than he was in the first two days, but that didn’t mean the receiver had more receptions. During seven-on-sevens, safety Andrew Mukuba was quick to Lemon on a stick route and nearly had an interception after running through the rookie. Later in team drills inside the red zone, a good play call got Lemon matched up against a linebacker on a short crosser in the end zone. Trotter hooked Lemon to the ground and was flagged for pass interference. Later, Jalen Hurts went to the receiver on a deep route out of the slot. Nickel cornerback Cooper DeJean initially was a half-step behind, but he closed on Lemon as the pass sailed out of reach. Lemon faced predraft concerns about his ability to get separation downfield. I don’t think those questions have been close to answered either way. But he clearly knows what he’s doing on underneath routes and carries himself with confidence, even if he got knocked around some on Saturday. Eagles training camp: 6 pressing questions after the first week of practices – The Athletic Berman: The Eagles haven’t slow-played first-round pick Makai Lemon into the lineup even though he missed minicamp. Lemon has been working with the first-team offense, and the Eagles seem committed to finding ways to get him the ball. Conversely, it hasn’t been that way for second-round pick Eli Stowers. He’s been down the depth chart at tight end and has yet to showcase his playmaking skills. I figured Stowers might be more involved in packages with the first-team offense. Why Eagles Teammates Are Impressed With Makai Lemon So Far in Training Camp – SI “It’s great to have them guys in my room,” said Lemon. “I’m the youngest guy there. I’m the only rookie. So, to have a bunch of guys in my room who have experience in the league, that’s the best position I want to be in. ”So, I’m going out there and asking them for advice, just how to do certain things, how to run routes, what they see because they’ve done it before, multiple times, at a high level. Me just being the student of the game, the rookie coming in, just trying to get all the information that I can.” Hollywood Brown shared a college head coach with Lemon, though at two different schools – Wicks at Oklahoma, Lemon at Southern Cal. “Makai works extremely hard,” said Brown. “He’s very detailed as well, and he’s tough. He’s competing every day. You guys see it. He gets hit, bounces back up and goes hard the next play. I’m impressed with him.” Go Birds! Radio, Part 1: Recapping Day 3 of Training Camp – Go Birds! Podcast James Seltzer, Eliot Shorr-Parks, and Bleeding Green Nation’s Brandon Lee Gowton are LIVE from the Jefferson Health Complex, recapping the third day of Eagles Training Camp. Radio, Part 2: Good Thing Philly Is A Defensive City – Go Birds! Podcast In the second part of Saturday’s radio show, James Seltzer, Eliot Shorr-Parks, and Bleeding Green Nation’s Brandon Lee Gowton react to the Eagles defense dominating the first week of training camp. Roob’s Eagles Observations: Are Nick Sirianni’s training camps really too easy? – NBCSP Britain Covey has caught more passes than anybody the first few days of camp. Why? Quarterbacks love throwing to Covey because he’s smart, he knows the entire route tree and he catches everything. Covey only has 13 catches in three seasons – six of them in one game against the Falcons in 2024 – and it’s hard to imagine him having a role in this offense, but he’s the perfect practice player because he’s going to make the quarterback look good. We all know how good a punt returner Covey is. His 11.3 average is 9th-highest among active NFL returners with at least 50 returns and 4th-highest in Eagles history (behind Ernie Steele in the 1940s, Brian Mitchell and Darren Sproles). His 11.3 is also 9th-highest in NFL history by a returner who doesn’t have a touchdown. Which tells you just how consistent he is picking up big yards without any huge returns. Covey is clearly on the roster bubble this summer. If he makes the 53, it will be because of his punt return ability. But he isn’t hurting himself catching the ball the way he has. 2026 NFL training camp: Top seven takeaways from Back Together Weekend Saturday – NFL.com It seems the split between A.J. Brown and the Eagles has produced better outcomes for both parties. Brown remains the talk of Patriots camp, where he continues to build a rapport with Drake Maye and cannot stop smiling, per ESPN’s Mike Reiss, while the vibes surrounding the Eagles’ offense in Year 1 under new OC Sean Mannion are much better entering the 2026 season. There’s a good reason for the latter: Quarterback Jalen Hurts might have more reliable protection in the new year. Guard Landon Dickerson, who battled injuries throughout much of 2025, spent his offseason working on recovery and physical preparation, leading him on a trip to Colombia for stem cell treatment that has him feeling much better as he embarks on another campaign. “Beautiful country, beautiful place. Trying to look to get treatment, keep my body healthy,” Dickerson said. “It’s my job, after all, so just exploring all avenues to try and feel good.” Meet the three-headed dragon in the Eagles’ secondary – PhiladelphiaEagles.com Quinyon Mitchell joked around with reporters after Thursday’s practice when asked about an ESPN article which listed him as the sixth-best corner in the league. Does he think he should have been ranked higher? “I don’t know,” Mitchell said while smiling. “It’s cool.” The third-year corner out of Toledo isn’t focused on outside noise – even after being named a first-team All-Pro. He has been in the Eagles’ facility this offseason getting stronger – both physically and mentally – getting back to the basics and working on his technique. Ahead of the second day of Training Camp, Defensive Coordinator Vic Fangio praised Mitchell’s work ethic. “I’m just trying to get better … every day I just put my head down at work,” Mitchell said of his coach’s compliment. “Each and every day I got to come out here, I got to earn my stripes.” “Did that mindset change at all? Earning All-Pro honors this past season?” A reporter…

summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers’ offense faced fourth down in the two-minute drill as rookie quarterback Drew Allar came to the line. The fans in attendance at St. Vincent College on Saturday came to life when a perfectly thrown […]
full_text: Jul 30, 2026; Latrobe, PA, USA; Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Drew Allar (16) participates in training camp drills at Saint Vincent College. Mandatory Credit: Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Pittsburgh Steelers’ offense faced fourth down in the two-minute drill as rookie quarterback Drew Allar came to the line. After taking the snap, Allar saw he had a one-on-one matchup downfield, launching a pass to A.T. Perry. The fans in attendance at St. Vincent College on Saturday came to life when a perfectly thrown back-shoulder pass was hauled in for a gain of nearly 40 yards to set the offense up inside the 10 yard-line. The same way they came unglued at the sight of a Will Howard 60-yard touchdown toss to Kaden Wetjen earlier in the week. The two young signal-callers knew all eyes were on them this week, and they delivered in what was as impeccable a start to training camp that the pair of Big Ten products – as well as the entire organization – could have asked for. The Steelers won’t take the practice field on Sunday, as they’ll have a day off ahead of putting the pads on for the first time on Monday. But in this day of reflection, it’s hard to imagine a better start for Pittsburgh in the acclamation period. On top of Allar and Howard playing a friendly game of “Anything you can do, I can do better,” their four-time MVP quarterback and star wide receiver are completely in sync. Aaron Rodgers and DK Metcalf have dominated in team drills, connecting on several completions at all levels of the field, highlighted by the Pro Bowl wideout giving rookie Daylen Everette a welcome to the NFL moment by going up and over him for a touchdown grab. Rodgers has also reminded everyone why he is considered by many to have the best pure arm in NFL history, threading the needle on multiple occasions, including a 25-yard strike to Pat Freiermuth in the end zone on Saturday. It hasn’t just been the offense having all the fun. Cornerback Asante Samuel Jr. has been the best player on the field on either side of the ball, breaking up several passes, two of which came against Metcalf. In the absence of both Joey Porter Jr. and Jalen Ramsey, Samuel has shown he is not just capable of playing a bigger role in the defense, but that he needs to have more reps on Sundays. And while if would be preferable to have both Porter and Ramsey on the field, seeing a potential star make his mark in their collective absence is a nice consolation prize. Now, this is the part where the perpetual pessimist scowls and practically races to scream something along the lines of, “YOU CAN’T LEARN ANYTHING FROM FOOTBALL IN SHORTS,” with about eight exclamation points to really drive the point home. And sure, we will learn more when the pads are on – especially as it pertains to the offensive and defensive lines. To say there can be nothing taken away from the first week of practices, though, is foolish. If everything had looked like a jumbled mess, those same pessimists would say the sky is falling. Had Howard and Allar looked lost, Mike McCarthy is a terrible hire and the Steelers may as well just not play the 2026 season. It’s okay to acknowledge when things are going well. And so far for the Steelers, everything is going as close to perfect as they could have asked for. Let us know what you think in the comments .
